speechtext: On the orders of the day:

subtopic: PROPOSED STUDY OF THEIR FINANCIAL SITUATION LOOKING TO EQUITABLE TREATMENT
speechtext: I should like to direct a question to the Secretary of State (Mr. Rinfret). I wish to ask whether the government have given consideration to the resolution introduced some time ago by the hon. member for St. Mary (Mr. Deslauriers) with regard to giving some relief to property owners in urban centres. The minister accepted the resolution at that time and said the government would give consideration to the problems of these people who find themselves in difficult circumstances. I know there are many cases of distress; many people are losing their homes because of high taxation and high interest rates. I assume the government have given consideration to this matter, but I should like to know definitely. I am asking this question to-day because I have a letter from a lady in my own riding telling me that her husband has been sick in bed for the last fifteen months, that she is forced to pay seven per cent on her mortgage, and that she is having some difficulty. I think some consideration should be given these people, and I hope something has been done by the government.

The house in committee of ways and means, Mr. Sanderson in the chair.
Customs tariff-267. Crude petroleum not subjected to any other process than natural weathering and removal of foreign matter and water, when imported by oil refiners to be refined in their own factories:-
(i)	-8155 specific gravity (42[DOT] 0 A.P.I.) or heavier at 60 degrees Fahrenheit: British preferential tariff, free; intermediate tariff, free; general tariff, free.
(ii)	Lighter than -8155 specific gravity (42-0 A.P.I.) at 60 degrees Fahrenheit, per gallon: British preferential tariff, 4 cent; intermediate tariff, J cent; general tariff, 1 cent.

Mr. Chairman, I rise
merely to make a few observations with respect to this item because it has been the subject matter of much discussion, and it is well that the circumstances under which the matter was referred to the tariff board should be upon record in Hansard.
It will perhaps be recalled that in October, 1930, the government of the day, having raised the tariff on gasoline and petroleum products, obtained from British American Oil Company, Limited, Canadian Oil Companies Limited, Imperial Oil Limited, and MeColl-Frontenac Oil Company Limited an undertaking in the following words:
The adoption of these recommended revisions will not result in any increase of prices to the retail consumer because of them.
Later the purpose for which that increase was made became apparent, although it was not fully apparent at the time. It was thought by some that it was done for the purpose of raising the price, but so far as that goes it is an illustration of the fact that raising the tariff does not necessarily involve an increase in the price of the product upon which the tariff is imposed. A statement to that effect will be found if one reads carefully the judgment of the tariff board. Beginning at page 183 you have the conclusions of the board upon the reference made by the Minister of Finance. On January 23, 1935, the former Minister of Finance, Mr. Rhodes, referred to the chairman of the tariff board by letter the application that had been received from the cooperative trading associations of Saskatchewan for a downward revision of the rates of customs duties on crude petroleum and its derivatives. Mr. Rhodes, after referring to the application that had been made, said:
Crude petroleum and its derivatives are enumerated, as you are aware, in a number of items of the tariff schedule comprising roughly a group running from tariff item 267 to tariff item 275 inclusive.
In the absence of a precise description of those particular derivatives of crude oil in which the applicants manifest an interest, I herewith refer to your board as reference No. 84 the group of items above referred to for inquiry and report in accordance with the terms of the Tariff Board Act.
In accordance with the reference then made the board not only received evidence at Ottawa, but also travelled as far west as Van-
Customs Tariff

couver and heard testimony at various points: at Regina, March 25-27, 1935; at Vancouver, May 20-21; at Calgary, May 27-29; at Saint John, June 17; at Halifax, June 20, and at Ottawa for the fortnight commencing November 19 and ending November 30.
The judgment of the board was delivered this year. The opening paragraph I propose to read, as well as a few other paragraphs, in order that the record may be complete. At page 183, chapter 13, the conclusion states as follows:
The customs duty of 2i cents per gallon levied on importations of gasoline in September, 1930, was undoubtedly an emergency tariff necessitated by the chaotic conditions in the oil industry in the United States at that time. It -was in the nature of a temporary measure pending a more mature consideration of the problem.
Then follows a record of the conditions in the United States during prior and succeeding years, the various movements of prices up and down, and the position at the end of 1934, when-
... the stabilization program enabled the integrated refiner to earn a fair profit. But the fixity and inflexibility of crude oil prices as compared with the changes and reductions in the market value of the products obtained from the crude oil seriously injured the nonintegrated refiners.
Then there is a further reference to the conditions in 1934, showing the improvement during that year and indicating that the retail prices of gasoline were higher by about ten per cent, or 1-J cents per gallon, because of the increased price of crude petroleum.
Unquestionably since the spring of 1935 conditions in the oil industry have definitely improved. Crude oil prices are at a level which would appear to permit the greater part of the current supply of oil to be produced at a profit without offering too much inducement for new drilling.
After reviewing further the conditions in the United States in the mid-continent field and the price structure of crude oil, upon which the production of gasoline depends, the board went into the question of the condition of the Canadian companies and of the profits which they had made, and at page 188 occur these words:
It will be remembered that the two main purposes of tariff protection, as stated by one of the major oil companies and quoted in the introduction of this report are:
(1)	To regulate imports to such an extent as to permit Canadian industry to benefit by increased throughput, with the resultant advantages of mass production;
(2)	To protect Canadian industry from competition from other countries where conditions of manufacture, distribution or economics differ from Canadian standards or conditions, whether this be due to unusual, unfair, unsound or unlawful practices.

It has already been shown that the chaotic conditions in the United States oil industry involving unusual and unlawful oil practices no longer exist, and that the industry as a whole is in an extremely sound position. The conditions of manufacture are not unlike those in Canada, except in so far as the refineries in many cases have a much larger capacity. But there are a number of refineries with capacities comparable to those in Canada which compete with the larger refineries and which operate in many cases, so far as their supply of crude is concerned, under conditions far less advantageous than do the large Canadian refineries.
There is necessity for protection against a refinery like the Royal Dutch Shell Company's refinery at Curasao in the Dutch West Indies, which has a capacity of over 200,000 barrels per day, and whose costs are said to be lower than those of any refinery in the United States. Other items to be considered are the higher costs of materials and the higher equipment costs in refining operations. Prior to the Canada-United States treaty, the average rate of duty on refinery machinery was approximately 35 per cent, although this increased costs amounts to only a small fraction of a cent on a gallon of gasoline. Nevertheless the board sees no reason for the continuation of these protective rates on refining equipment which is so extensive and expensive.
The refineries in the prairie provinces pay extremely high freight charges on the crude oil which is transported to the refineries by tank car, but they have a freight advantage of over two cents by reason of the higher freight rates on gasoline.
Climatic factors involving more expensive buildings, the insulation of tankage, and the burying of pipe lines to a depth of six feet below the frost level, warrant a certain measure of protection. The fact that water transportation to Montreal and Toronto is unavailable for five months of the year thus necessitating large crude oil storage, must also be borne in mind as an item requiring protection.
So far as the first purpose of the tariff, as stated by the oil company, is concerned, the increase in the tariff in 1930 had the directly opposite result. Although the share of the market held by Canadian refineries increased approximately 15 per cent in 1934 as compared with 1930, the Canadian industry did not benefit by increased throughput with resultant advantages of mass production. The number of refineries increased from fifteen in 1930 to forty-two in 1934 and the percentage of capacity in operation declined from 72 per cent in 1930 to 55 per cent in 1934.
After dealing with the labour element, which the board states is not important, having regard to the value of the industry-the employment does not amount to more than 5,000 people-they point out that they have rewritten the schedule with a view- to modernizing the phraseology in accordance with commercial usage, and deleting words and phrases which have become obsolete. I continue reading:
In the chapter dealing with the tariff history of the items comprising the petroleum schedule, it was pointed out that certain items are substantially the same, so far as wording

Customs Tariff
is concerned, as they were in 1884. As new products have been developed, additions have been made to existing tariff items, with the result that petroleum products are frequently classified with crude petroleum in the same tariff items, and there are overlappings in the specific gravities named in certain items.
The board then proceed to suggest new tariff items, and deal with them on the basis of the American Petroleum Institute rule, which is an arbitrary rule settled by the institute, and which has been found satisfactory as to specific gravity. After giving that, the question as to where the break should take place becomes important. The board give in exact words the reasons why the break was made at the point it was. I shall have something to say about that presently. To continue:
Under the existing schedule, the bulk of the crude petroleum imported by refiners is imported under tariff item 267a. The number of that tariff item has been altered to tariff item ^ 267 (i) and the words "in its natural state" have been deleted on the grounds that if an oil is crude petroleum, it must be in its natural state. The qualifying phrase "not subjected to any other process than natural weathering and removal of foreign matter and water" is added to assist the customs authorities in the administration of the two divisions of tariff item 267. When the crude oil comes from the well, foreign matter and water are usually removed before it enters the pipe line or storage tank.
It will be noted that in the existing tariff item 267a, crude petroleum -7900 specific gravity (47[DOT] 6 A.P.I.) or heavier is specified, whereas under the proposed tariff item 267 (i), the upper gravity limit is -8155 specific gravity (42-0 A.P.I.). Under the proposed tariff item 267 (ii) crude petroleum lighter than this gravity when imported by refiners carries a rate of i cent under the intermediate tariff.
There are several reasons which seem to the board to justify a reduction of the gravity denoting the dividing line of demarcation between dutiable and non-dutiable crude oil for several reasons. In the first place the crude oil which is available in commercial quantities in the United States has an A.P.I. gravity of 40 degrees A.P.I. or less, and prices are posted for every degree change in gravity from, say, 25 degrees A.P.I. to 39-9 degrees A.P.I., and one price is posted for 40 degrees and above. The fact of the matter is that the higher gravity crudes are obtainable in comparatively small quantities, and the prices quoted for these oils are not necessarily based on any fixed ratio to the gravity as in the case of the oils having a gravity below 40 degrees A.P.I. As stated in a previous chapter, the price of crude increases 2 cents per barrel with each increase of 1 degree in the gravity. Fixing the dividing line at 42 degrees A.P.I., gives the refiners a margin of two degrees in gravity.
Secondly, the reduction of the gravity limit of crude petroleum, entitled to free entry for refineries, will prevent certain refiners from importing under the "Free" crude oil tariff item mixtures of gasoline or petroleum tops with crude petroleum. There has been considerable difficulty through mixtures of "tops" and crude oil dutiable under the present tariff item 267b, or crude oil and gasoline being invoiced as crude petroleum in its natural state under tariff item 267a. This can be done very easily when the gravity limit is 47-6 degreees A.P.I. (-7900 specific gravity) as at present. The limiting of free importations to 42 degrees A.P.I. gravity and heavier, would remove the possibility of evading the duty. The wording of the new item will also eliminate the practice of shipping mixtures and billing them for freight purposes as crude petroleum "in its natural state."
The third and most important reason, however, is that crude oils with a gravity above 42 degrees A.P.I. are in reality "freak" crudes which are not available in sufficient quantities to supply the market requirements of gasoline. The normal crudes below 40 degrees A.P.I. require expensive "cracking" equipment to obtain a similar quantity of gasoline to that obtained by a simple skimming process in the case of high-gravity crude oils.
For example, with a crude oil of 47-6 degrees A.P.I. the yield of gasoline by a "straight run" operation is as follow's.

I shall not read further, but I have read from the record because I believe it is desirable to point out that the difficulties to which the minister referred w'ere not difficulties which have arisen recently, but were those which had arisen in 1934, and formed part of the cause operating in the mind of the minister who referred the matter to the tariff board. The difficulty did not arise in western Canada, in the first instance; it arose in' eastern Canada in connection with a cargo of oil from Russia and subsequently a cargo of oil from Roumania. The oil was invoiced as crude petroleum in its natural state, when as a matter of fact it consisted of so-called crude oil
Customs Tariff

mixed with gasoline which had been refined in very excellent refineries, as the product clearly indicated, and it was only necessary to put it through a simple process to separate the gasoline content from the crude oil content of the importation.
I recall clearly having asked officials of the Department of National Revenue whether or not there was any method by which we could deal with the matter, and it was then learned for the first time that in some particulars the classification in the tariff had not been changed since 1884, and, as was suggested the other day, there was no method by which we might separate the contents of the so-called crude petroleum for purposes of duty. It became apparent that it was necessary to revise these classifications in order that fraud could not be practised upon the revenue collections by invoicing as crude petroleum a product which was more largely composed of gasoline than of crude petroleum. It was that circumstance which brought the matter first to the attention of the department. Subsequent investigations by the Department of National Revenue resulted in what was indicated by the Minister of Finance. But the cause which brought about the difficulty to which I referred was the importation by water of a petroleum product invoiced as petroleum in its natural state, when as a matter of fact, it consisted of crude petroleum mixed with high class gasoline. That was one of the reasons which brought about the necessity for referring the matter to the tariff board.
The other reason was that complaints were made that the duty was enhancing the price. As is pointed out in the judgment of the board, it is quite clear that that could not have been the purpose of the imposition of the duty. The purpose w,as to deal with the chaotic condition which existed in the United States and to secure at no increase in price the necessary gasoline produced in Canada for Canadian consumption. Side by side with the increase in tariff it will be recalled that a new section was added to the tariff which enabled the governor in council to place upon the free list any commodity that had been increased in price by reason of an increase made in the tariff itself. I shall read from page 191 of the record what the board has to say on this point:
Having carefully considered the various elements of cost which are higher in Canada than in the competing countries, the board has arrived at a schedule of rates which in its opinion, having regard to the return of normal conditions in the United States industry, will permit the Canadian refining industry to do business in an economic and efficient manner.

These are the words to which I wish to direct particular attention:
The very wording of the pledge given in 1930 to the government by the major oil companies to the effect that the retail price to the consumer would not be increased because of the customs duties, implied that the companies did not require any more than one cent duty on gasoline because of differences in manufacturing costs here and in the United States. They needed the additional one and a half cents to protect the Canadian market against the chaotic conditions in the petroleum industry of the United States _ already described. If they required the increased protection on manufacturing costs, they would have had to increase prices to the consumer.
As a matter of fact they kept their pledge; there was no increase in the price of gasoline consequent upon the tariff. Any increases in gasoline prices that took place in this country were increases that marched side by side with the increase on crude oil as set out in the judgment of the board.
I make this statement because the tariff of 1930 was imposed for one purpose, and one only. It accomplished that purpose, and it did not thereby involve any higher price, as the board itself has found. There were no increases in prices by reason of the tariff. Such increases as did take place were increases in the cost of the raw material as reflected by the prices posted from time to time in the area from which the crude comes. The difficulty in this country is that we have not as yet discovered any pools of crude petroleum. We have what is called casinghead gasoline or naphtha, discovered in the Turner valley and produced in extensive quantities. It is a high grade product, so high grade in fact that at times you can fill your tank with it right from the well and drive your engine with it. But the quantity is not sufficient to supply the requirements even of western Canada, although the consumption of gasoline in this country last year as given in this report was, I think, only about 500,000,000 gallons, which of course is relatively a small quantity as compared with United States consumption, especially when we recall that one refinery of the Royal Dutch is capable of producing 200,000 barrels a day.
In my judgment the result of the new tariff proposals will be to protect, so far as this indicates that protection is necessary, the interests of those engaged in refining in this country. The minister referred the other day to the objections that had been made in Montreal and elsewhere with respect to the decrease in duties. I think those who were complaining overlooked one essential fact. The fact was not that the protection was not ample from the point of view of prices, but that it was not ample from the point of view of permitting a possible importation into this

Customs Tariff
country of gasoline from countries that were willing to sell it at almost any price. Remembering that Russia was not in the hands of private enterprise and that they were offering gasoline for sale in the city of Baltimore at as low, I believe, as three cents a gallon, in a tanker, aDd having regard to the fact that on a barter basis oil from Roumania was offered in this country at a very low price, what the president of McColl Frontenac Oil Company had in mind, if I can understand what he said, was-

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: It was a little difficult to understand.

Well, I read it in the light of just what this judgment says, that is, not that there was not ample protection with respect to competition on a price basis, but that chaotic conditions in the industry elsewhere might involve the importation into this country of gasoline at an invoice price so low as to make it impossible for the moment to compete with it here. I will give an illustration of what I mean.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: My right hon. friend was very generous in interpreting the comment in that way. I mean he was generous to the man making the comment.

The reason I read the undertaking to which the McColl Frontenac Oil Company was a party in 1930 was to show that that must have been in the speaker's mind. I have no other reason for saying it, because I have not spoken to anybody about it, but it occurred to me that he gave the undertaking that the price would not be increased by reason of the tariff. Clearly, as was pointed out in the judgment of the board, it was the chaotic condition that prevailed and the sale at what may be called bankrupt prices of gasoline in Canada which made it impossible to carry on the sale of gasoline in this country with any stability unless there was some, certainty as to the prices at which gasoline would be imported from countries where chaotic conditions prevailed. I recall its being brought to the attention of the government that between 1930 and 1934, a large concern in the United States, which had a great tank farm filled with gasoline, pledged to the bank, had been unable to meet its obligations; the bank had been compelled to take over the tank farm, and they offered the gasoline at a price that would liquidate their debt, and were content with that. The obvious result of such conditions was that unless we had imposed the duty we did, namely 21 cents, a serious situation would have developed. To
permit that gasoline to come into Canada without restriction would have meant for the moment a lower price to those who bought it. But there were those who were speculating in gasoline who were willing to buy it in tank cars, sold as it was at distress prices by reason of the bankruptcy of the concern owning it, and, by bringing it into Canada and selling it at a lower price, disorganize the price structure in this country.
The board has apparently given a tremendous amount of time and care and attention to this matter. Anyone who has any preconceived prejudices with respect to the oil industry, and will take the trouble to read this judgment, realizes why prices in Canada have varied from time to time. It is because we have no raw material from which we can produce our finished product. We can secure raw material only in three ways: by tank cars, by one pipe line only that comes into Canada, and by water. In the summer time water carriage is available to Montreal and Toronto, and ships do carry tank oil up to the refineries in Toronto and it is there refined, but for five months or more in the year that is not possible; therefore, except via Halifax and Vancouver, where you have water carriage the year round, you must depend entirely upon tank cars. It is stated in this judgment, touching a matter with which we in western Canada have some concern, that the higher freight rate on gasoline arises by reason of the lower rate on wheat; it is a compensatory tariff for the railways by reason of their carrying the wheat at a much lower rate than prevails in the United States for the transportation of similar grains over similar distances.
I read the comment to which the minister referred the other day as indicating that the higher tariff was not required for the purpose of protection in the sense of increasing the price to the producer, but solely for the purpose of preventing distress gasoline from finding a market in this country and thereby disturbing the stability of the whole structure. That was the ground on which the case was put to the government in 1930. It was for that reason that the undertaking was obtained that the oil companies would not increase the price by reason of the tariff, and, as the judgment points out, obviously the increased tariff serves no purpose if any duty higher than the cent a gallon is necessary for the purpose of maintaining the industry in this country. The adequacy of the protection-if you wish to use the word protection-at one cent a gallon is quite clear. The higher rate is for the purpose of protecting the industry
Customs Tariff

against sporadic inroads of the kind which came about by reason of chaotic conditions in other countries-at that time, in the United States. Anyone who has followed the history of the industry in the United States as set out in this single volume will realize how uncertain those conditions have been, and if you add to that difficulties that have arisen by reason of importations by water from the Black sea and Roumanian fields, you get a truer and clearer appreciation of the situation.
I followed with some degree of interest the statements made by the hon. member for Moose Jaw (Mr. Ross) who has apparently given the matter a great deal of consideration. I have no opinion with respect to the question of freight rates, but I do know it was because of the conditions to which I refer that this matter was referred to the tariff board in the hope that with improved conditions in the industry it would be made apparent that all that was aimed at by the government was not to increase the price of gasoline to the consumer, but to try to secure for him a steady, certain price that would not represent undue profit on the part of the producers. An effort was made to guard against destruction for the moment by spasmodic and sporadic inroads upon the market by those who were not permanent Droducers, but -who were launching their pro-iucts in the markets of this country for the purpose of raising money-not being a regular industry in that sense-by liquidation of bankrupt concerns, or by countries overseas attempting to realize needed money to meet their economic needs through taking advantage of trade and exchange difficulties.

Such investigation as I have been able to make in connection with this duty on crude oil leads me to express commendation of the Minister of Finance (Mr. Dunning) for the sincere effort he has made to help the consumers in the west. A great many people in the west have signified to me their appreciation of this action. I should like also to commend the minister for the statement he made the other day, which appears on page 3018 of Hansard, that he was directing the tariff board to follow closely the reactions which might follow from the application of this changed tariff. I believe that this is a very sound procedure and I commend the minister heartily for his action in that regard.
There is another matter to which I should like to direct the attention of the minister. In Alberta at the present time are two smaller companies which import gasoline. These

companies are laying down gasoline in Calgary at such a price as would seem to indicate that they are perhaps making greater profit than should be made; consequently it might be a good thing if the minister would direct the tariff board to send a representative to Calgary to investigate this matter. I believe that this would be a good starting point. Once more I express my appreciation of the activities of the Minister of Finance in connection with gasoline prices.

I should like to say
just a word in connection with the point of view expressed the other afternoon by the right hon. leader of the opposition (Mr. Bennett). When speaking to this particular item on AVednesday last I suggested that in my opinion the method of handling the alleged abuses in connection with the importation of light crudes was fundamentally wrong. AVhen the leader of the opposition was expressing his opinion very logically and very ably, I felt that he was emphasizing the point of view I had expressed that day.
Protective tariffs are brought into being in order to protect the price levels of certain classes of producers in Canada, but unfortunately other classes of producers are not protected from the chaotic conditions of the markets outside of Canada. The result is that a product produced in a protected market has to be sold under chaotic conditions abroad. Consequently there is opposition to this method of affording protection from unfair competition by means of protective tariffs. There is also an urge that the government of Canada should reciprocate in another form and assure the primary producers of Canada such prices for their products as will be equivalent to the prices guaranteed by the tariff to those who receive the benefits of it. That is what I intended to develop the other afternoon when six o'clock was called.
I believe the Minister of Finance is adopting an unsound method of dealing with the alleged condition in relation to certain refineries, which he outlined to the committee. The widespread use of this method of dealing with such situations will make the condition as far as the western producers are concerned one of confusion worse confounded. AA7hat-ever we may think of other features of the matter, I am thoroughly opposed to increasing the tariff as a means of dealing with this particular situation. May I emphasize again that in the best interests of understandings between all groups of people in the country, it would be wise for the government to consider a method of dealing with this particular matter different from the method proposed by the Minister of Finance at this time.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext:
While I do not want to obstruct the passing of one of my own items,
I should like to say that in my opinion the most important point made the other day in the discussion with respect to crude petroleum had to do not with the tariff but with the fears expressed by several members that advantage would be taken by the railway companies of the new classification in the schedule to introduce higher freight rates on the lighter crudes than prevail in connection with the other crude oils. It will be recalled that the other day I expressed some doubt as to whether that would be possible in the light of a judgment of the ralway commission already of record, especially in view of the fact that in the old petroleum schedule there were at least three separate crude items whereas in this tariff there is only the one item with two minor divisions. It was apparent to all who discussed this matter that any injury which might be done to the so-called small refiners, which I prefer to refer to as skimming plants, would be done not because of this half-cent rate in the intermediate tariff, but because of a possible increase in the freight rate which might be brought about as a result of the divided classification. In that connection I gave certain assurances with respect to the tariff board watching the situation during the coming year. I am in a position today to go a little further. The chairman of the tariff board received this morning a letter from Mr. L. J. Knowles, special traffic representative of the Canadian National Railways, from which I quote in part. Mr. Knowles says:
I have this morning discussed, by telephone, the situation with Mr. R. W. Long, our general freight traffic manager, and I am authorized by him to make the attached statement to you so far as the Canadian National Railways are concerned, and the substance of this statement may be used in any manner that you see fit, publicly or privately.
I had better read this statement because of its immediate interest. It is as follows:
So far as the Canadian National Railways are concerned, there need be no fear whatever that any attempt will be made to increase the freight rates on crude oil of the higher gravities-or even the lower gravities-from the Texas or Oklahoma oil fields to western Canada.
Of course, these rates are joint international rates, and the Canadian National Railways have no authority to speak for the United States lines, but we do not believe that they also will attempt to make any change in the rates on account of the differentation in the duty which has now been made by the Canadian government.
This assurance is given predicated on the understanding that the oil shipped from the Texas and Oklahoma oil fields to western Canada will be genuine crude oil in its natural state, for the following reason:
Last year the United States railways became so concerned about doctored crude oil (which is often a mixture of gasoline, distillate and crude oil) being shipped as crude oil at the low freight rates which were established originally on the heavy crude oil for use in cracking plants, that they determined to make a change in the freight classification which, up to some time last year, designated crude oil as crude oil and nothing else, so that under the freight tariffs it was possible to ship crude oil in its natural state, or crude oil not in its natural state, as crude oil.
With the cooperation of the American Petroleum Institute, and with the approval of the Interstate Commerce Commission, the United States freight classification, which also applies on international shipments, was changed to read as follows:
"Crude oil in its natural state, or crude oil which has been subjected only to natural weathering, settling or treatment for the removal of water and bottom sediment, and not blended with other products."
The very language we are using in the tariff item.
This designation is shown on page 285 of the consolidated freight classification No. 10, which both the United States and the Canadian lines are parties to.	[DOT]
The effect of changing the description as designated, is as follows:
Crude oil in its natural state, or which has only been subjected to natural weathering, and so forth, and not blended with other products, may be forwarded over the United States and the Canadian railways on bills of lading which will authorize the use of the rates on crude oil wherever they may apply in the freight tariffs in which the rates are published, which freight tariffs are subject to the governing clause of the consolidated freight classification No. 10.
Therefore, if the skimming plants in western Canada buy genuine natural crude oil and have it shipped to them from Texas and Oklahoma to western Canada, there will be no question that the rates which the Board of Railway Commissioners authorized in their decision, after an exhaustive investigation, will apply.
If, however, the shippers or receivers want to sbip crude oil not in its natural state, that is, crude oil blended with other products, they can honestly describe it as crude oil not in its natural state on the bills of lading, and the rates applied will be the ordinary petroleum rates which apply on gasoline or gasoline mixed with other articles.
Of course, this means that crude oil not in its natural state will pay higher freight rates, but the fact is that this condition has been in effect now for over a year.
For example, crude oil in its natural state from Tulsa, Oklahoma, to Regina will continue to pay a rate of 53J cents per 100 pounds, which was authorized by the Canadian railway commission in its decision.
If the shipment is offered as crude oil not in its natural state, that is, gasoline distillate and crude oil, it will pay a rate of $1.23 per 100 pounds, as the railway tariffs provide that a mixture of high grade and low grade articles take the highest rate on any article in the mixture.
This is a well known principle of railway rate making, which is recognized by both the Canadian railway commission and the Interstate Commerce Commission.

There is a further matter which should be mentioned in this connection, and that is, if any shipper or any receiver of crude oil not in its natural state, or blended with other products, wilfully and knowingly attempts to ship that particular kind of alleged crude oil as crude oil in its natural state, they will not only be subject to the additional ordinary rate between the proper crude oil rate and the petroleum products' rate, but they will be subject to prosecution under the Interstate Commerce Act or the Canadian Railway Act, or both.
The situation, therefore, as explained, is, so far as the freight rates are concerned, thoroughly cleared up, and no one need have any fear that, so far as the Canadian National Railways are a factor in the situation, there will be an increase in freight rates on crude oil from Texas or Oklahoma to western Canada as long as they are honestly shipping natural crude oil, no matter what the gravity may be.

I wish to quote some of the remarks he made-and curiously enough they appear at page 1924 of the second volume of Hansard of 1924:
Then there are others like myself who believe that it is in the national interest that we should have diversified industries. I am willing to place agriculture first and to give a prominent place to all the industries that deal with the development of our natural resources; but I will also say that manufacturing must take a very prominent part in the essential industries of Canada if we want to build up a nation with an all-round development such as we ought to have. Such men believe that a tariff
may be used to maintain and to encourage industry, even though sometimes it may be, apparently, at some slight sacrifice. They believe that if Canadian workmen are to be paid good wages, that will enable them to live decently and comfortably, in many lines of industry they cannot compete on an even basis with the underpaid workmen of foreign countries.
These noteworthy remarks of the present Minister of Trade and Commerce, who was a private member in 1924, are just as sound to-day as they were at that time. Good wages cannot be paid by the Canadian manufacturer unless he has a substantial sale in his own home market for the things which he produces; and unless he has some means to protect himself against the low wages of some countries and the tremendous output of mass production plants in the great republic to the south. The hon. gentleman continued-I am quoting only what bears on the point I am making:
There are men-and I am one of them-who believe in a moderate tariff that will maintain Canadian industry. I believe in that as a wise policy. If that makes me a protectionist then I shall have to accept the designation. But I will also say that I do not particularly like the word "protection." In its original meaning it is beneficent and benevolent in its significance, but it has been so abused that it has acquired something of a sinister meaning.
I agree with the description of protection which the hon. gentleman gave on that occasion, and perhaps the word has been abused. I have always been of the opinion that if a tariff, the primary object of which is to provide employment, were carried into effect, there is no reason why the government could not regulate prices. I am not in favour of exploitation; I am not in favour of allowing manufacturers to charge exorbitant prices, and I see no reason why any government cannot protect the consumer, because the purpose of the tariff is not to permit the charging of exorbitant prices but to provide employment for Canadian workmen. I quote once more from the hon. gentleman's remarks :
I do not favour a prohibitive tariff but I believe in a tariff that will enable legitimate industries to live if they are efficiently conducted. I believe in that sort of tariff also for another reason, namely, that it will give employment to our people.
In my opinion that is the primary purpose of a tariff, to give employment to people. I have gone around a number of implement plants and recently I have seen hundreds of men working in one branch of production or another, and I could not help feeling that it was my duty on every occasion to say a word on their behalf.

The government has at this session given considerable relief to our western farmers in more waj's than one, and I support it in what it has been doing to make conditions better in the west. Quite a number of measures have been proposed, all of which I hope will result in better conditions there, because anyone who really knows anything about economics-and practically every member in this house does-knows that if the primary producer is not successful the whole country takes a backward step. If, therefore, the government does anything to improve conditions for the farmers it will have my support.
Going around industry, and with such knowledge as I have of industry, I find, as has been pointed out by other members, that the amount of agricultural equipment produced in this country is very small indeed in comparison with what is produced in the great factories of the United States. A few days ago I was going through the establishment of one large company. I have a thorough knowledge of industry, particularly of anything associated with iron and steel. I saw something that I had not realized before in connection with the agricultural implement industry, and that is the large number of jigs they have to use. I saw several large bins of them, and the estimate of the foreman was that they had 5,000 different jigs in that one plant for use in connection with drilling, pressing, or otherwise working up and getting ready the various items that enter into mowers, binders and all other agricultural equipment. In addition to that, they had a lot of equipment for the pressing of malleable iron. It appears that when the malleable iron parts used in various agricultural implements are received from the malleable iron plants, though perfectly constructed, they are not always true to shape and it is necessary to use dies to press them out. I counted over four thousand dies in one plant, and naturally these extremely costly dies and jigs are two of the reasons why agricultural implements may cost a little more to produce in this country than in the United States. Where an agricultural implement plant in Canada would use a die to press a thousand parts for a thousand implements the American plant would use a similar die to press perhaps fifty times as many, so naturally they can produce for less money. If the government really wants to do something for the farmers, and at the same time not destroy the agricultural implement industry, let it develop some plan whereby equipment, costly dies and jigs, such as that used by manufacturers, not only in the agricultural implement line but in other lines,

may be obtained at low cost, just as the government provides seed grain and one thing or another for our farmers.
I have been over a good deal of Ontario recently, and I can see where the steel makers of Owen Sound and other centres, who make bolts, nuts, bar iron and one thing or another for agricultural implement plants, are going to have less work. They cannot have more work when we see paraded in United States newspapers articles stating that shipments of goods of this kind to Canada are increasing. Every thousand additional parts made in Chicago or some other United States city for Canadian farmers means less employment in this country, and so all along the line. I think every member of this house, if he is not thoroughly familiar with what is manufactured in his own riding, should make himself familiar with it, and on behalf of the workmen in his riding rise in his place and oppose the importation of goods similar to those made in his riding. Take the city of Yarmouth, in Nova Scotia, I do not know if the hon. member representing that riding is in the chamber at the moment, but in that city there is, I am informed, an excellent plant which makes the duck and canvas that goes on the binders, one of the best lines of canvas made anywhere. A completed binder brought into this country fully equipped with canvas and everything else just takes away that much work from the Yarmouth plant. If a thousand binders are brought in it means that just that amount of work is taken away from the men employed in that plant. Then, in Montreal they make the tubes and other articles to which I referred a few moments ago. To-day agricultural implement firms in Canada are buying a large part of their requirements from this Montreal plant, which I believe is called the Canadian Tube and Iron Company, or some such name. Every hundred men engaged in Pittsburgh making that line of material for binders to be shipped to this country will displace a hundred men in Montreal or some other Canadian city. I cannot see anything else to it, and so it goes with all these items.
In the town of St. Mary's, Ontario, a very fine little town, at one time they made a large line of agricultural machinery. They are not now making a full line but they are making a number of small lines of excellent material. That company formerly made binders, mowers, side delivery rakes of a very high grade, hay tedders, hay loaders and so on, but they have had to discontinue manufacturing many of these articles and whether or not they have as many men engaged to-day as they had ten years ago I do

not know. Certainly when they had to discontinue many lines the number of men employed must have been reduced. The same applies to plough makers in Woodstock Brantford, Aurora, Owen Sound and many other cities and towns in Canada. I know very well that nothing I can say can alter any of these items; the government appear determined to crucify this industry to a degree. I do not say that they are doing so intentionally or that their motives are not sincere. I will admit that they are sincere, but nevertheless the jobs of a great many workmen in this country are in jeopardy as a result of these nine or ten items pertaining to agricultural machinery.
I should like to see some government reverse this policy and do as the late President Roosevelt did when he introduced the tinplate industry into the United States. This is the way in which the story has been told to me; I cannot vouch for it, but I assume it is true. He sent for various steel and tin makers and asked them if they could roll steel to the gauge of tinplate. They said that they could. Then he asked if they could provide enough tinplate and galvanized iron to supply the market in the United States. They said that they could not, without a tariff. So he asked, according to the story, "What tariff do you want to enable you to manufacture tinplate and galvanized iron in the United States in order to take care of this market'? They told him how much they wanted. I do not recall just what the rate was, but the story is that he said, "Well, we will advance that higher. We are going to try to have American workmen supply the tinplate and galvanized iron used in this republic, but we will not allow you to exploit the American buyer." In that way it is said that the American tinplate and galvanized iron business became established.
I do not see any reason why we cannot prevent exploitation, nor can I see why the jobs of these fine, solid machinists, blacksmiths and fitters of one kind or another engaged in the production of the hundreds of lines of material that enter into the construction of agricultural implements should be jeopardized in this country merely because it is said that agricultural implements are too high in price. It is an easy matter to regulate the prices of agricultural implements without crucifying the industry, but it seems to me that is what this tariff will do. In order to encourage hon. members representing ridings in which there are substantial plants to take a stand on this issue, I want to read some newspaper comments on a speech delivered by the present Minister of Trade and Commerce
(Mr. Euler) in connection with the budget of 1924. I quote from the Toronto Mail and Empire of May 10, 1924:
Mr. Euler: I say that is a policy which I cannot support

Mark you, Mr. Chairman, the present tariff lowers the duties even further than was proposed in 1924 with regard to ploughs and the other machinery included under item 409c.
I say that is a policy which I cannot support, if the words of the Minister of the Interior reflect the considered policy of the government, and it is a policy against which I must protest in the interests of my constituents-
May I interrupt? I am not anxious to go into ancient history, twelve years ago, but will my hon. friend state what he is reading from, or what the reference is?
It relates to the budget of 1924.
The deatlvknell of protection.
Yes, I assume that is what it was.
Well, my hon. friend should know, because that is important.

This present tariff is on the way to be the death-knell of industry.
-it is a policy against which I must protest in the interests of my constituents.
I would like to see other hon. members rise in their places and protest in the interests of their constituents. The hon. member for Trinity (Mr. Plaxton) should be on his feet, representing the large number of men who work for the Massey-Harris company. The minister continues:
I cannot make that protest either consistently or effectively by speaking one way and voting the other, and for that reason I propose to vote against the budget.
Continuing, the minister said:
Party allegiance should be something apart from tariffs, Mr. Euler believed. "If my views on the tariff do not let me call myself a Liberal, my lifelong conception of Liberalism has been incorrect."
I congratulate the minister on having said those words, and I should like to see other hon. members on the government side, representing not less than one hundred to one hundred and fifty substantial companies of this country whose businesses are going to be seriously affected by the lowering of these agricultural implement duties, rise in their places and use those noble words that the present minister used in 1924.
I want to say a word further about the workmen. A movement is commencing at present
Customs Tariff

through which I believe that workmen in the plants in Ontario and elsewhere will establish a defence of their jobs for themselves. There are so few who stand up and defend the worker and his job, which has been seriously affected by so many asking for the lowering of duties. I have in my hand a placard, addressed to the workers in the plants. I hope that before this year is out every industrial institution in Canada will plaster its shops from one end to the other with information to enable its workmen to do something on their behalf to understand the tariff. This placard reads:
Your Business
Your job depends on Canadian tariff rates preventing unfair competition from workers in other countries.
These tariff rates are set by the members of the dominion parliament at Ottawa.
Your member of parliament should know what the textile tariff means to you.
He is your personal representative. He votes for you when the tariff rates are decided.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext:
Does my hon. friend
approve that?
Approve what?

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: That sort of thing?

I approve workmen
becoming conversant with what provides a job for them, and the defence of their jobs. I realize that if 20,000 workmen in the United States make goods for shipment into Canada which are now made and can be made in Canada, that displaces 20,000 workmen in Canada.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext:
That, of course, is not
at all the question I asked.
And I approve the average workman becoming conversant with any information that will enable him to have a knowledge of what enables an employer to give him a job.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext:
Will my hon. friend be
good enough to tell me what institution posts that kind of notice in its plants, and will he place the whole notice on Hansard?

Yes, I will place this
notice on Hansard.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext:
And the name of the
concern?
The name of the concern is not on it.

The organization that put
it out?

I do not know the
organization that put it out. But I do not see anything wrong. Why should not the workmen of this country 'become conversant with the benefits of the tariff? It is high time they did.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext:
That is not making
them conversant with it.

Of course it makes them conversant with it, by directing their attention to the study of the tariff. I do not see anything wrong with that. I am not in accord with anything that gives any further trouble to the government in these trying times; on the other hand I am in favour of whatever will provide employment. My life has been different from that of many hon. members. I have associated with thousands of wTorkmen for many years. I have seen many men laid off and taken on, and I have always made up my mind that I would raise my voice in support of anything that would provide more employment. Agricultural implements are only one line; I hope they can continue in existence, but if they cannot, I shall be sorry. The government know what happened to many plants in 1924. Someone said something about the good times that came after the tariff of 1924. I know that in September, 1924, a large delegation, manufacturers from all over, Toronto and elsewhere, came to Ottawa to attend what was called an unemployment conference. I do not remember who called it but they met here to try to suggest ways and means to provide employment.

Where was my hon. friend
last year when the industrial and international relations committee was sitting and I wanted Canadians hired on our ships?
Well, I have been in the house right along: I am one who is generally in his seat.
I have missed the hon. member out of his seat many times.

The hon. member is
out of order; he is talking about a committee I was on and a report which I supported, as I assume the hon. member did.

The hon. member did not
support it.

In closing, I want to
tell the minister that I do not question his sincerity in the action he is seeking to take; he is perhaps doing what appears to him best. On the other hand I hope he will grant my

Customs Tariff
sincerity from my background of long association with workers and my firm conviction that I should on all occasions do what I can to defend the employment of workers. I do know this, that when a plant has a thousand men working there are a thousand contented families. I was associated myself with a plant that formerly had nine hundred men on its payroll, and to-day, not as a result of anything the government did, that same plant has, I believe, about one hundred men. That is not a line of goods which has been affected by the tariff; this situation is due to conditions of the times, perhaps.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext:
We are not guilty of
that one?

No; the minister will
admit I have given, him credit for many things, and I hope that whenever I can say a good word for what anyone is doing, irrespective of party, I shall do so. On the other hand what I have said is based upon my experience and observation of a number of agricultural implement plants, seeing what they are up against; they are trying to keep going but they fear that they may not be able to do so.

I have always been interested in hearing the hon. member for Davenport (Mr. MacNicol) discuss the different questions that come up in connection with our tariffs, and the interests of the workingmen. I suggest every hon. member should be interested in the working man and the agriculturist. Representing an agricultural constituency, I am aware of the situation in which the farmers find themselves. When one goes among these people it is most discouraging to find that they are scarcely able to make ends meet, to say nothing about being able to enjoy the comforts of modem conveniences, to which they are certainly entitled.
When the government take action of this kind in connection with the implement industry I am quite sure they have no intention of trying to injure the workman. They are attempting to better his position and also that of the agriculturist, who is engaged in the greatest industry in Canada to-day. If the hon. member who has just spoken is so concerned about the workman-and I am going to confine my remarks to the agricultural industry-then I think he ought to read the records of what happened after 1924, when the tariff was reduced. I am quite satisfied that if the reduction in tariff made at that time had thrown thousands of people out of work, as we are asked to believe, the government at this time would not be putting the duty back to where it was in 1930.
Would the hon. member permit an interruption.

Just a minute; I do not often speak in the house. The hon. member has said that we ought to have a reversal of the present policy. We had! that in 1930, when the tariffs on these commodities were raised materially. We had an increase in the tariff on binders amounting to 300 per cent and in that on seed drills amounting to 233 per cent. We could go through a long list of items, showing a complete reversal of policy in 1930. I take it that the hon. member is concerned about the workmen, as I am. I have a keen interest because I spent most of my life in the industry. The report of the price spreads commission shows that the average number employed in the implement manufacturing industry for the years 1931, l932 and 1933 was 3,878, whereas in the two years preceding 1931 the figure stood at 9,068. The average number employed in the nine full years between 1922 and 1930, was 8,780. According to the bureau of statistics in the years 1931, 1932, 1933 and 1934, the average number was 3,500. The average wages and salaries paid in the nine years between 1922 and 1930 is given as $1,206, while the average in the years 1931 to 1934 stood at $1,010. The average production for the nine years I have indicated is given as $31,723,000, and that for the latter period stood at only $7,457,000. In 1929 there were sixty-two plants operating and in 1934 only thirty-five.
The hon. member for Greenwood (Mr. Massey), in speaking a short time ago, indicated that 18,000 jobs were in jeopardy. Today the hon. member for Davenport has asked why so many jobs should be jeopardized. I should like to place on record figures given to the price spreads commission showing the numbers employed in the industry. The hon. member for Greenwood said, "I say to-day that the jobs of 18,000 men are at stake. Yes, and how many more jobs are there at stake in industries which contribute raw material?" I take it for granted from the hon. member's statement that there are 18,000 jobs in the industry itself. The report of the price spreads commission indicates that in 1929 the total number employed in four of the largest agricultural implement concerns was 10,408, and in the ten smaller concerns, the sections of the industry which represents over ninety per cent of the production, 708 were employed, making a total for that year of 11,106. In 1933 there were 3,880 employed. When we refer to the number employed, what do we mean? First of all, we have the factory workers, and we find that in 1929, there were 7,276 employed, whereas in 1933 there were
Customs Tariff

only 1,989. In 1929 there were 172 employed in factory administration, and in 1935 there were 105. In 1929 there were 1,201 clerks employed, and in 1933 only 515. In l929 the figure for selling, or for agents, is shown as 1,709-5 and in 1933, it is 832-6.
The table is interesting from the viewpoint of the worker. Hon. members who have spoken have shown great concern for the worker, and may I say that he is the man in whom I am interested. Further than that, I have a great interest in the farmer who, under present conditions, is scarcely able to exist. We find that in 1929 in the four large industries executives salaries averaged $7,394, and wages to workers averaged $1,219. What was the situation in 1933? In that year the executives still had the high average of $6,512, but the average for the factory worker, the man who produced the goods, was reduced to $837. If we take the figures indicating what happened between 1924 and 1930 and those for the period from 1930 to the time the figures were given to the price spreads commission we must agree that during the previous years the worker was in a far better condition than he was when a duty of twenty-five per cent existed. That must be the conclusion, if we are going to attribute it all to government interference with tariffs.
I submit that the figures are all against those who contend that the worker is going to lose his job if .the tariffs on implements are reduced. So far as my personal experience is concerned, the best years the country had were when tariffs on implements were the lowest, and the best years the farmers had were when tariffs were the lowest. I am sure that the chief concern of the government is to help the worker and also .to help the agriculturist-. My hon. friend referred to what happened in 1924. He said tariffs were reduced and disastrous results followed. What are the figures? We find that, according to the bureau of statistics, in 1924 there were 6,700 employed in the implement business; 1925, 7,559; 1926, 10,091; 1927, 11,011; 1928, 10,867; 1929, 11,408; 1930, 7,405. Then we come to the time when the tariff was increased. If that was calculated to help the situation it should be reflected in the figures.
Will the hon. gentleman repeat how many were employed in 1930, the first year of the depression?
There were 7,405.
That was the first year of the depression. The hon. gentleman seems to forget all about the depression.
I am not forgetting about the depression. I have been in this business for thirty-five years. In 1931 the number employed was 4,471; 1932, 2,758; 1933, 3,039; and 1934, 3,706.
Improving.

That was the situation with reference to the employees. I want to be fair, but if the tariff itself was to be the means of providing these men with work, as was promised in 1930, it absolutely failed, and if a reduction in the tariff was calculated to throw men out of work, as we were told in 1921, the figures show that the very opposite happened. I remember the debates and discussions that took place in 1921 as to what would happen if these tariffs were reduced. But these figures tell the story better than any discussion on the platform or anywhere else.

The -hon. member recalls what happened in the election of 1925, I
suppose?
I am not concerned with what happened in any election. I am citing these figures.
Oh, give us some figures of your own.

I could do that. Let us see what happened to capital. In 1924 the capital invested in the industry was, in round figures, $82,000,000; 1925, $81,000,000; 1926, $78,000,000; 1927, $88,000,000; 1928, $91,000,000; 1929, $103,000,000; 1930, $98,000,000. In 1934 it was $55,000,000. Let us consider the amount of wages paid after these "disastrous" tariffs were brought into effect in 1924. In that year-I am giving round figures-salaries and wages were $8,000,000; 1925, $9,000,000; 1926, $12,000,000; 1927, $13,000,000; 1928, $13,000,000; 1929, $14,000,000; 1930, $9,000,000; 1931, $4,000,000; 1932, $3,000,000; 1933, $3,000,000; 1934, $3,000,000. If anybody, in face of these figures, can stampede the industrial worker, he can do more than I would ever attempt to do or than I think anybody should attempt to do.

I think one should provide some antidote to the speech of the hon. member for Davenport (Mr. MacNicol). In my opinion the reductions that have been made in the tariffs on farm implements are to be welcomed and the government is to be commended for having made them. I should

Customs Tariff
like to have seen implements put on the free list, and the hon. member for Davenport provided me on one occasion with what is perhaps the best argument which has yet been made in the house for such a proposal, in stating that the cost of a group of five implements at Hallock, Minnesota, was higher than the cost of the same implements at Emerson, Manitoba.
We have heard a great deal about the workers. The hon. gentleman who has just taken his seat (Mr. Golding) gave some very interesting figures regarding the salaries and wages of workers during a number of years. When I was a boy I was brought up in an atmosphere of political discussion, and the particular subject that was keenly debated in my boyhood days was Mr. Chamberlain's tariff reform proposals. I well remember it used to be said that we need not worry about a tariff because the foreigner paid the tax. Well, then I bought a ticket to Canada, and I found that in this protected country the people of Canada paid the tax. But here I encountered an entirely different argument, namely that it was necessary to have the tariff to foster our infant industries. That was twenty-six years ago, and apparently the argument still persists that we should have the tariff to protect industries which are infants and need some protection; that is particularly true, of course, of the agricultural implement industry. Yet we find that the industry is one of the largest in Canada and that a considerable percentage of its output is sold in foreign markets where it has to compete with that of other countries. Consequently, it seems to me, the industry should have reached the adult stage by this time and we might quite safely leave it alone.
Though I should like to have seen implements placed on the free list, I am not going to make a motion to that effect, as I did on another occasion, because I believe that the government is to be commended for having gone so far as to reduce the duty by 17i per cent in one year, and that we should see exactly what the reaction will be in the next few months. I should like to point out that only industries which are well organized and have reached the stage of trustification can possibly maintain prices at a high level in the face of decreased protection, and it seems to me that implement companies have made a very serious mistake, from their point of view, in increasing the prices of their products when the tariff protection was reduced. I think, if this continues, the government should take the appropriate steps to see to it that advantage in this way is not taken of the present situation.
I do not propose to say a great deal more about the matter except that I know the figures given a few moments ago by the hon. member who immediately preceded me are correct, because I looked them up. I have noted one point. Whereas the managerial end of the. industry maintained the salaries that were being paid, the ordinary, common run of the workers took very substantial cuts. I worked this out in connection with the four largest companies, and I find that fifty managerial employees received 2-57 per cent of the total wage bill in 192$ and 7-51 per cent in 1934. In the ten smaller companies the rate was something like nine per cent in 1929 and fifteen per cent in 1933.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: Did that come about by increases?
No; there were decreases.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: Uneven decreases?

Yes; the cuts fell more heavily upon the lower paid people. This fact was brought out by the price spreads inquiry: The more highly protected an industry, the worse the conditions in it. I do not say that this is true of the agricultural implement industry; I make that as a general statement. This has been found to be so in the textile industry. In connection with the. discussion on crude oil I stated that the producers of western Canada had to buy in a protected market while they had to sell in markets where there was no protection. The producers of western Canada are not in a position to buy implements to-day. A short time ago the hon. member for Winnipeg North (Mr. Heaps) said that we should let antiques come in free. If things go on as they have been going, many of these producers in western Canada will have to import antique implements in order to obtain repair parts, and I suggest that they be allowed to come in duty free. I just rose to say we in this corner are glad to see the reductions and we hope they will be reflected in the price levels to our producers.

I had the privilege of speaking in this committee on May 5 in defence of the workers engaged in the farm implement industry. I spoke out of a deep sincerity of purpose and with some knowledge of the facts. Since that date I have listened to many discussions, both in and out of this chamber, relative to the points covered in my remarks. I have the highest regard for the integrity, honesty and well-meaning purpose
Customs Tariff

of those who speak in this chamber, and that which I have to say now is said out of that regard.
The hon. member for Huron-Perth (Mr. Golding) referred a moment ago to several matters in connection with the implement industry which to him appeared to be salient and important. He had perused some figures given him by the bureau of statistics, and he referred to other figures as well that told a story which he interpreted in the way he disclosed this afternoon. Again I say that I do not for a moment doubt the sincerity of purpose behind that interpretation and I know my hon. friend will not misunderstand me when I say that figures on paper, taken without knowledge of the facts behind them, are insidiously dangerous and may be terribly misleading. I heard the hon. member refer to 1924; I heard him refer to 1929; I heard him refer to 1930, and right up to and through 1936, without a single word of reference to world conditions. I heard him refer to implements in 1924 and to implements in 1936 as if he were speaking of the same implements. I repeat that it is very misleading merely to consider figures on paper without a knowledge of the facts back of those figures. There were low duties on farm implements in 1924, in 1926, and up to 1929; it is true that the business of Canadian companies increased, but the hon. member made no mention of the reduction in the duties on raw materials going into those implements.
I am in favour of that too.

The hon. member made no mention of the reduction in the duties on raw materials; he made no reference to the fact that a preference in duty was given to the manufacturers of farm implements by way of a reduction from 37^ per cent to six per cent as far as their raw materials were concerned. When the hon. member was referring to the increase in the business of Canadian companies, did he mention the increase in the business of other companies? Did he mention that that increase was out of all proportion to the increase in business of Canadian companies? It is very simple to attempt to defend an argument with figures on paper without reference to the facts. What percentage of increase in farm implement business did the Canadian companies enjoy compared with what was enjoyed by other companies?
Why did the hon. member challenge the figure of 18,000 which I gave as the total number of men engaged in the implement industry? I propound again that that figure

is absolutely accurate, even in the face of the figures from the bureau of statistics quoted by the hon. member. These figures, I assume, do not include agents, agents' helpers and so on. Let me take a hypothetical case. Here are two men who are depending for their livelihood upon their jobs. Here is one man depending for his livelihood upon his job. Is not the principle involved in taking away the jobs of the two men exactly the same as that involved in taking away the job of the one man? What matter if it is 18,000 or 9,000, the principle is the same, so why debate the exact dimensions of the figure?
One cannot help being alarmed when he considers that this is an old and established industry, made up of various companies within it, which has made a magnificent contribution towards the development of this country but which is threatened to-day without a chance being given to it to make representations on its own behalf. I am not standing in my place here this afternoon for the purpose of taking up the time of this committee, for the purpose of objecting to what that one said or what this one said, or for the purpose of having some words of mine recorded on Hansard; I am here with all the earnestness of which I am capable to urge upon the government, as I did before, the fact that there are those who regard it as hopelessly unfair when the criminal is apprehended and sentenced before his trial.
That would not matter if he is a criminal.

Would you take the law into your own hands and say that he should be sentenced before his trial?
Hon. members were no doubt interested in hearing from the hon. member for Rosetown-Biggar the respective percentages of the earnings enjoyed by those who work with their head and their hands and those who work with their heads. The hon. member for Rosetown-Biggar (Mr. Coldwell) compared from memory the percentage of salaries paid compared with the total moneys paid by the implement industry in 1929, I believe, and in 1934. In 1929, it was two per cent, was it not?
Compared with-

-in 1934. I am -not here
to speak for the man who is an executive alone, not by any means. I worked up from the factory to an executive position in the implement industry and I felt that my salary

Private Bills
was far too low; in fact I knew it. There are those who hold positions of importance in the implement industry who, in my estimation, may at times have received salaries higher than should have been paid. I felt so at the time and feel so to-day. But I submit that it is unfair to the industry as a whole to take the percentage of salaries of executives in one year and to set that percentage beside the percentage of salaries paid in a year of deep depression, when naturally the number of those who are in factories and in other fields where wages are paid is reduced. In one company alone of which I know, $5,000,000 of so-called head office expense and other savings along that line was taken out per annum, in times of depression when hundreds are employed instead of thousands. The executives to whose salaries reference has been made this afternoon by the hon. member for Rosetown-Biggar have had reductions of ten, twenty, forty and perhaps fifty per cent, but the men are still there; for someone must conduct the executive responsibility of the business.
The question of foreign markets for the implement industry as a whole has been a most difficult one. Questions of exchange, questions of this, that and the other have come into the whole picture, making it necessary for some companies, if they wish to maintain their business in foreign countries, to change their method of distribution and perhaps of manufacture. Then the question is asked in this chamber: Why is it that if a Canadian company cannot compete in its own country it can compete in a foreign country? I had hoped that my attempt to make this clear, when I spoke in this chamber on May 5, had registered to stay; but the very fact that in the United States last year the volume of business was twenty times what it was in Canada, and the very fact that we are right next door to the United States, make a colossal difference to the one who manufactures and sells in Canada. But if one goes to some foreign country where sales are relatively small, where even large companies compete on the same basis as small companies, for the reason that their selling organization is not nearly so large proportionately in that country, then I postulate that the picture is entirely different.
We face in the implement industry in this country to-day a far different situation from that which prevailed in 1924 and in other years before 1929. As I say, the whole picture is changed. Millions upon millions have been spent by the implement industries in both this and other countries for the development of machines; millions have been spent in this 12739-194
and other countries for the maintenance of service, which has not been permitted in one iota to vary in its efficiency at all times even when sales were dropping and the bottom was falling out, and this not in Canada alone but to an even greater degree throughout the world. There has been a challenge to the industry to maintain itself through these years and the industry has done so.
I have the highest regard for the farmer and the keenest appreciation of his problem, and any measure which can be introduced on his behalf and for his benefit, which is not only in his interest but in the interest of the country as a whole, I endorse every time. But why is it there is always this fiendish glee in pursuing the implement manufacturer, who seems to be regarded by so many as the arch villain of the piece? Three dollars out of every hundred dollars spent by the farmer is spent for implements. I tried to point that out the other night. Why do we not pursue some of the other manufacturers who furnish the farmer with goods? In this chamber I read a list showing that articles in everyday use on the farm are priced per pound higher than implements are priced per pound, and an implement lasts anywhere from ten to fifteen or twenty years. I myself have serviced a binder cutting its forty-fifth crop. Why this relentless pursuit of the implement industry alone? Does the implement industry itself hold in its hand the key to the success of the farmer? Does this industry alone hold in its hand the key to his failure?
