subsubtopic: PROPOSED ABOLITION OF HANGING AS DEATH PENALTY
speechtext: Mr. Speaker-

subsubtopic: PROPOSED ABOLITION OF HANGING AS DEATH PENALTY
speechtext: I would direct the attention of hon. members to the fact that if the hon. gentleman speaks now he will close the debate.

subsubtopic: PROPOSED ABOLITION OF HANGING AS DEATH PENALTY
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I will endeavour to be brief, for various reasons. In dealing with this question of the abolition of hanging and the substitution therefor of the lethal chamber, there are different theories of punishment that come to mind. The first is retribution; the next is the theory of deterrence; the next is the reformative theory; the next is the educational theory; the last is the theory of disapprobation, and sometimes there is restitution.
In dealing with this question previously we discussed the theory of retribution, and we did not hear anyone approve hanging for the purpose of retribution. That is the old theory, an eye for an eye and a tooth for a tooth, the theory that a man should be punished because he deserves punishment. That is looking backward, punishing a man as a fact and not for the benefit of the social order. We feel that this old dispensation has gone, and I was glad to note that hon. members did not approve that old theory of retribution. That was the theory which prevailed in Scotland when they massacred one another; it was the theory of the guillotine in France, when they beheaded one another, but that theory has now pretty well disappeared.
Then we come to the theory of the deterrent effect of punishment. The strange fact about punishment is that the more we progress in knowledge and intelligence the greater becomes the sphere of crime. Crime is the product of the social order, and it seems that the higher we rise in the social order the greater amount of crime we have. The tendency has been that though crime has become largely extended the severity of the punishment, broadly speaking, has decreased. At one time, not so many years ago, in Great Britain there were two hundred crimes for which people could be hanged. To-day there are only four or, practically speaking, only one, that of murder. The deterrent theory is perhaps the most important question to be considered. It has been suggested during this 
debate that we punish people for the benefit of the social order, and this theory is much to be preferred to that of retribution. We have a utilitarian motive, as Bentham expresses it; we punish for the purpose of preventing similar wrongs by others against the social order, so we think the deterrent theory is good. But that theory has to foe watched carefully, 'because we can make errors in it. For instance, if the deterrent theory is beneficial, why not have all hangings in public squares, as was the case long years ago? That finally met with the disapproval of the public; we found that it was a detriment to the social order, so hangings were carried out in private places. I think that was a correct move to make.
The next question is whether we should punish so severely as to cause pain. I still have the utilitarian idea that pain has no beneficial effect. If we are not punishing for a purpose, then to inflict such punishment as to cause pain is a sin against humanity. If we can punish the victim and at the same time improve him; if we can punish him so that the punishment will bring about an educational reform, that might be different. I would not be opposed to punishment of that kind, but when we punish a victim on the edge of death, when no benefit can be derived, I think that policy is entirely wrong..
I have 'before me many expressions of opinion from different associations and organizations. I am not going to take time to read them all, but I should like to make some-reference to a few. I have a communication from the Ontario sheriffs' association, as follows:
That in the opinion of the sheriffs of Ontario in convention assembled, the method of inflicting the death penalty in use in Canada is a relic of mediaeval days and the advance in humanitarian civilization calls for the substitution of a more human method. Furthermore in our opinion a central place in the province should be provided for imposing the death penalty, thereby ensuring and facilitating the proper administration of justice and materially reducing the considerable cost to the public of the present gruesome method.
This is from the Halifax Herald:
Here is a case where a man from another province invades a peaceful local community, murders and robs a respectable and almost helpless citizen, and sets fire to his house in the hope of concealing the crime, which he has now confessed. Notwithstanding his confession this man will still have to receive a formal trial. A jury will have to be summoned for the purpose, and very considerable cost incurred, most of which will fall on the ratepayers of a municipality which has been deeply sinned against instead of sinning. But there is worse than that to follow. If the

Criminal Code-Death Penalty
accused should be convicted, his execution will follow as an additional and most distressing burden on the officials of that municipality. This is conspicuously unfair and unjustifiable. There is no modern excuse for it. If a less sentence than that of death were imposed on this or any other criminal, the convict would at once be removed to a central penitentiary to undergo punishment. Only in the case of murder is the municipality compelled to provide for the execution of the court's sentence.
Then I have a letter from Arthur Ellis, the hangman. He says:
I would deem it an honour to be able to assist you or any other responsible party in the attainment of this humane reform. This question, I am led to believe, will come up for discussion at the interprovineial premiers' convention in Ottawa next week, but I am sure on account of it being of great importance it will be shelved to be taken up by some committee who really know nothing of the situation or of this serious matter....
Arthur Ellis trying to have hanging set aside 1
I might refer to the experience of other countries. I have opinions from many other countries and from many states of the United States. Some of the states still approve hanging. The state of Connecticut changed to the electric chair, as did the state of New York. A number have changed to the lethal chamber.
I have letters from most of the provincial premiers approving the change in our method of punishment; the only one who seemed indifferent was Mr. Taschereau, of Quebec. His letter reads:
I am in receipt of your letter of March 26, regarding the best method of executing criminals.
I beg to state that I have no set opinion on this matter. Hanging is perhaps not a most humane method of executing criminals, but it is after all perhaps the best deterrent, and this, to a great extent, is what society has in view in instituting capital punishment.
I have a letter from Arizona, which has changed to the lethal chamber; a letter from Colorado strongly approving the lethal chamber; one from Wyoming; one from Nevada which I think I should read because some criticism was made of their methods. This is from the attorney general:
There was a great deal of discussion and quite a good deal of criticism of this method of inflicting the death penalty in such cases in this state when it was first adopted. This criticism resulted in quite a thorough investigation of the method and of its effect on those who were subjected to the death penalty by means of lethal gas, by prominent physicians both of this state and some of our neighbouring states. After quite a thorough and extensive examination by such physicians of the first 12739-194i
few instances and first few persons who were subjected to this penalty, these physicians determined that this was the most humane method known by which the death penalty was inflicted.
I greatly appreciated the fact that the Minister of Justice (Mr. Lapointe) the other day spoke with some approval of this bill. I was glad to notice that the hon. member for Winnipeg North Centre (Mr. Woodsworth), the hon. member for Broadview (Mr. Church), the hon. member for Fort William (Mr. Mclvor), and the hon. member for Hamilton West (Mr. Wilton) also spoke in favour of it. The hon. member for York South (Mr. Lawson) spoke to some extent in opposition, but still he made a statement which I think is helpful, as to the deterrent value of punishment. He said that the greatest deterrent is the certainty of prosecution and the certainty of punishment in case of conviction.
The leader of the opposition (Mr. Bennett) criticized this proposal and said:
We must not forget that those about whom we are so solicitous were not solicitous for those whom they destroyed. When they wreaked their vengeance, by murder dark and foul, they were not thinking of the pain they caused or the injury they did; they were not thinking of the sorrow they caused to those who survived. In this age there are always-manifestations of our becoming victims ofi maudlin sentimentality and thinking in terms of the pain and suffering of one whom we are removing from society because of his offences against it, but at the same time I suggest that we should never forget those who have suffered because of the offences which have been committed.
I think the leader of the opposition was wrong in one or two of those statements. I think we should forget, if possible, the one who is gone. We should direct our attention to the social order to prevent a repetition of similar crimes. This idea of stirring up sentiment because of the killing has to do with the theory of retribution, which should not be present in our law courts or in our arguments on this matter. The leader of the opposition accused some of us who support this bill of maudlin sentimentality. That, I think, was a very unfortunate word, and I rose to correct him at the time. "Maudlin" comes from the French spelling of "Madeleine" which refers to the sympathy of Mary Magdalene. We have the approval of a higher authority than the leader of the opposition for the sympathy of Mary Magdalene. I hope I am one of the victims of that sentiment; I think it would be a good thing if many of us had more of the Magdalene's sentimentality and sympathy for the poor classes. I think the leader of the

opposition used that word without realizing the seriousness of its implication.
Now, Mr. Speaker, this bill has received much approval from most hon. members I would say, who have expressed their views. It has been suggested by the Minister of Justice that I should withdraw it until the matter can receive further consideration, and I think that is the proper method. This question should not be dealt with hurriedly; it is a serious matter and should receive due consideration. I am delighted to think that the Minister of Justice is prepared to give it such consideration. He has suggested that I bring it up at the first week of the next session. When the committee took recess at six o'clock I was speaking of some questions in the minds of many relative to the situation in regard to the farm implement industry, as a part of the whole picture of Canadian industrial and economic life. I have only a few more words to say, but to me they are exceedingly important and I hope hon. members will feel the same way.
One cannot remain long in this august chamber without realizing with crystal clearness that throughout this vast dominion we have a series of sections, the outward manifestations of which are found within those sections. One realizes there is a group here, another group here and another here across the dominion, possessing points of view peculiar to themselves and points of view which to them are exceedingly precious. It is difficult indeed, particularly for western farmers, to catch the point of view of the eastern industrialist. In turn it is difficult for the eastern industrialist to catch the point of view of the western farmer.
We are Canadians, and as such we are interested in the fullest and best for this Dominion of Canada. No one section is pitting itself against another or striving for any supremacy peculiar unto itself. It is to be sincerely hoped that, according to the sentiment so ably expressed on more than one occasion by the Minister of Finance, there will be built up within Canada a feeling of confidence in the country not only as a country but as a producing country, producing

the products of the farm and those of the factory. It would seem to me that any step taken further to sectionalize this dominion, or further to give expression to the desire of one part to achieve for itself at the sacrifice of another, is after all that which must be regarded as definitely unfortunate. The eastern manufacturer finds it difficult to understand why the western farmer demands that certain things be done when, as a result of those very demands, the eastern workman realizes that his job is in jeopardy.
Those of us who take a keen interest in the affairs of the country-and that means all hon. members and many thousands of people outside this chamber-do not want to see injustice done to any one section. If-and this is only an assumption; I do not concede it for a moment-the implement companies have been unfair and have functioned in a manner which has brought about the exploitation of the farmer, then indeed those implement companies should be brought to task. Thus it was that when it was sounded from coast to coast that there was to be a committee to investigate the implement industry and to make a report, both sides of the house were satisfied. For, indeed, it was felt that the offspring of that body would be conceived and born in fairness. To-day I believe that committee still sits. To-day the tariff on farm implements has suffered its second reduction since the first of the year.
I postulate that this condition brings about an unfairness which is felt in the manufacturing east, while the primary producing west hopes that it may bring a reduction in implement prices and, judging from what has been said by hon. members, regardless of the effect on industry in the east. In all sincerity and deepness of feeling, speaking as one representing a constituency in which industrial workers make their homes, I ask that due consideration be given this great question, for indeed it is a great one. Nine thousand men engaged in industry-or is it 18,000? I say it is 18,000. Regardless of whether it is 9,000 or 18,000, let us say: "Here are 9,000 breadwinners"; "Here are 18,000 breadwinners"-what matter the number? The principle is the same. I would be remiss in the responsibility placed upon my shoulders if I failed to stand in my place and to raise my voice in urging the government to reconsider this tariff item.

given the answer, and I am afraid that if the hon. member cannot understand it I cannot do any batter. The result of the high price of farm implements is that our factories are closed. I am not going into statistics, but that is the actual effect of high prices; no farmer can afford to pay them. The implement manufacturing companies close their factories and discharge their employees. The figures prove that; it is apparent to every hon. member. My hon. friend from Davenport (Mr. MacNicol), whom I must compliment upon his ability to defend his constituents at every opportunity, is concerned about the workmen. The reason the factories were closed and we had so much unemployment was that the implement firms would not reduce the price of their farm machinery, and, it being a non-perishable product, they were able to fill their warehouses full of it, hold up the price, close the doors, and wait till the farmers bought it. But they did not expect the depression to last as long as it has lasted, and perhaps in the long run they have suffered more than the farmers.
May I ask the hon. member the authority for the last statement he made? Or is it a personal opinion?

No. Here are the figures: In 1930 there were 7,504 employees in the agricultural implement industry. In 1934 the number was 3,706. I think that proves that

when the factories closed their doors they discharged their employees and aggravated the unemployment situation.

The hon. member stated
that the implement manufacturers were able to hold up the price of their implements and fill their warehouses, and therefore the farmer was not able to buy, which, of course, in my humble estimation, is a totally incorrect statement.

I do not wish to make an incorrect statement. I am satisfied that the farmers were not able to buy the implements, and I know the factories did not continue to manufacture, because they could not sell, and if they did not continue to manufacture, I do not think they would be likely to retain their employees, although they did retain the majority of their executives.
Was not the depression the cause of that?

I agree with my hon.
friend to the extent that I think it had a great deal to do with the matter; that is, the depression among the farmers.
More than the farmers.

Hon. gentlemen on the
other side of the house fail to realize the depression in agriculture. When there is depression in agriculture there is depression all along the line. The agricultural industry is not in a thriving condition at the present time, and it needs farm implements. I think the best illustration of our condition is to tell the committee that last fall I was in a farmer's yard; the men were tinkering at an implement, and one of them said to the boss, "We will have to get another carload of hay." He said, "Surely the hay is not done yet." "No," said the other, "but we are out of haywire." That is the condition of the farm implements on the majority of the farms of western Canada. The farmers have patched them and patched them again, and tied them up with haywire until they are in such a condition that the farmer must either quit or buy new machinery. But the facts prove that the agricultural implement manufacturers decided to raise their prices and take advantage of the farmers in their dire necessity. That is my opinion, and I think I am justified in holding it.
I do not intend to offer many more observations. I thoroughly agree with the hon. member for Greenwood when he says that this is a big country and that we should be working in the interests of every one in

it, and not for any particular class. The machine companies and the farmers are interdependent; the welfare of the one depends upon the welfare of the other, and instead of having strife with these or any' other companies, we should work in cooperation. When the value of farm products went down as it did in 1930 and during subsequent years, why did the machine companies not reduce the price of their implements so that the farmers could continue to buy, and thereby assist in keeping the factories open and giving employment to the people of Canada? That is where the farm implement companies made a mistake, and now they are paying the price. I hope they have learned their lesson, and I invite the hon. member for Greenwood, who represents the agricultural implement industry, to-

May I again interrupt?
I do not represent the agricultural implement industry. I speak for the workmen in that industry.

The hon. member mentioned the industry so often in his speech that I thought he was making a special plea on behalf of it. I believe that he mentioned the employees as well. The hon. member for Rosetown-Biggar (Mr. Coldwel!) is not always complimentary to the present government; yet he was big enough this afternoon to confess that they were marching in the right direction. He gave the government credit for the reduction in the duty on agricultural implements. I want to say that I concur most heartily in that remark of the hon. member and I want to congratulate the government upon reducing the duties on agricultural implements to 7J per cent. I think this reduction was warranted and perhaps we could go further. In view of the attitude of the agricultural implement companies in increasing prices, notwithstanding the fact that the duties had been lowered, I think the government of the day would be justified in cutting the duty off entirely and putting these implements on the free list. We have had free entry into the United States for a considerable number of years, and if countervailing duties are wanted, why not have them apply to agricultural implements? In view of the attitude of the farm implement industry, I think the government would be justified in wiping out the duty altogether.

Might I ask the hon.
gentleman a question?

My hon. friend's question can come later; I want to give the full thread of this story. I think my hon. friend will find that it is really charming if he can only see it in the right light. There then came a change and the right hon. leader Of the opposition (Mr. Bennett) came into power. He said that it was necessary to save the industrial fabric of the dominion. I am not sure that he was not thinking of the textile industry; he was getting his fabrics mixed. We will let it go at that.
What followed? Down to 1933 there was a decline in industrial wages in the dominion, the drop totalling $348,000,000. I do not here and now contend that the lowering of the tariff in 1924 was responsible for the expansion of industrial activity in the dominion during the next five years. I do not raise that contention at the moment, but I ask my hon. friend from Davenport to sit down and look at the history of that period. When he does that I challenge him to come before the House of Commons and say that because the government of that day lowered1 the tariff industry was paralyzed. Will he go back to the people in his own constituency of Davenport and tell them that? Does he think the people of that constituency will accept it? I wonder that he can look the Davenportians in the face after a speech of that kind and after he has told them that their industries were ruined.
May I ask the hon. gentleman a question now?

I do not know of any other hon. gentleman in this committee who never for a single second yields to the suggestion of lower tariffs, but the hon. gentleman from Davenport never does. This afternoon in a moment of kindness the leader of the opposition suggested that at least in one item the tariff was too high. I am reminded of the words of Dryden, who spoke of one Shadwell of his day as follows:
Shadwell alone, of all my sons, is he,
Who stands confirmed in full stupidity.
The rest to some faint meaning make pretence,
But Shadwell never deviates into sense;
Some beams of wit on other souls may fall,
Strike through, and make a lucid interval;
But Shadwell's genuine night admits no ray;
His rising fogs prevail upon the day.
I should like to transpose that a little and say:
Some beams of wit on other souls may fall.
Strike through, and make a lucid interval;
But Davenport's genuine night admits no ray,
His rising fogs prevail upon the day.
Now may I ask the hon. gentleman a question?
My hon. friend must wait until I have finished. The suggestion is that the agricultural implement industry was ruined by the advent of this policy in 1924.
Who suggested that?

The hon. member for Davenport suggested that. He was saying that all industries were paralyzed, so surely the agricultural implement industry must have felt the shock. From 1920 to 1924 the progress of that industry in the Dominion of Canada was in one direction. The number of employees decreased from 12,S00 to 6,700. Then the tariff was changed in 1924 and the number of employees increased year after year. They increased to 7,500, 10,000, 11,000 10,000 and 11,000. The hon. member for Greenwood (Mr. Massey) suggested that the total number of employees was 18,000, but he was counting every man who goes out from the Massey-Harris company to sell a binder or to fix one in the field. He assumes that if agricultural implements are not made in this country, none will be bought, none will be sold and none will be serviced. I return for one moment to the question of what would have happened in 1924 if the policy of the hon. member for Davenport had been put into effect.
There would not have been any delegations coming to Ottawa to ask for employment.

My hon. friend can follow me in just a moment. He is as a pillar of cloud by day and a pillar of fire by night. If what my hon. friend claims is correct, then in 1924 the advance made by

this industry would have been more rapid than it was under the Liberal government. Does my hon. friend contend that? Will he suggest that to the house?
I contend that the lowering of duties in 1924 increased emigration and the number of delegations coming to Ottawa to ask for employment.
That is exactly what I want my hon. friend to say.

You have it.
Mr. DEACHMAN. Does my hon. friend contend that the increase in the production of manufactured goods would have been greater in the Dominion of Canada between 1924 and 1929 than it was?
Yes, if we had had an adequate tariff.

These are the figures. The total production stood at $2,695,000,000 in 1924 and it went up to $4,063,000,000 in 1929. Does my hon. friend say that it would have been still greater? Let me point this out to the committee. My hon. friends had the direction of affairs from 1930 to 1933 and they pushed the tariff up to the limit. There was no hesitancy or weakness on their part; they pushed the tariff up to the limit. What followed? Production dropped to $2,086,000,000 in 1933 from $4,063,000,000 in 1929. Yet my hon. friend says that it would have been higher if they had been in power. In other words, it would have risen to greater heights and crashed to greater depths and unemployment would have been greater. I ask my hon. friend to take that story back to Davenport. I ask him to admit what he ought to admit. He can answer me later; there will be lots of time to-night. He claims that if the tariff had been applied in 1924 we would have increased the volume of production and we would have had more men employed. A tariff cannot be made to do more than the tariff did in 1933, and production had crashed then to half what it was in 1929. It would have had further to fall and the destruction of the industry in this country would have been greater than it was.
I turn now for one moment from Davenport to Greenwood. I like my pleasant friend; never for a moment does he say an offensive word. But he stood in the house to-day as the one outstanding illustration of the failure of the policy of high protection in Canada. Why do I say that? That industry has been for years one of the key industries of this dominion. It has been held up as an industry which has developed as a result largely of protection. The protective tariff was first 
granted it because it was an infant industry and it was thought desirable to build it up in Canada. What followed? The hon. gentleman tells us that this infant industry was established some ninety years ago, and it has been followed by fairly high protection. The tariff got down to six per -cent on binders a few years ago, and when the Massey-Harris company appeared before the tariff board, at the time the iron and steel schedules were under inquiry, the representative of the company did not ask for an increase in the duty; they were ready then for a tariff of six per cent. After all these years, what has happened to the infant industry? Old and experienced, with abundant capital and everything else, it comes before the house and declares that the infant industry day is gone; that the industry has passed that stage, and that now it wants something for its old age. Is that not a perfect example of the folly and uselessness of protection, when you pile tariff on tariff-

Will the hon. gentleman
allow a question?

Not now, please; I
should like to finish. My hon. friend from Greenwood says that he is worried about the worker. What worker? Is the man on the farm not a worker as well as the worker in the factory? What does the hon. gentleman plead for in this committee? He pleads for the idea that something shall be taken from the worker on the farm and something shall be given the worker in the factory. If it were possible to build up industry on that basis then his argument might receive consideration; but we have had fifty years of experience of high protection in Canada and we have found that in no single period in that time have we had real prosperity under high tariffs, whereas in every period when the tariff was reduced there has been an improvement in conditions.
My hon. friend appeals against sectionalism.
I would ask him to put this test to himself. The farmer in western Canada to-day produces grain that must be sold in the open markets of the world. He has no protection on that product, for he must take the price which is determined by open competition with every other producer. In that position he is without help; and my hon. friend says that, in order to avoid sectionalism in Canada, we should put the tariff 'back on agricultural implements so as to allow the manufacturer of those implements to take something from that farmer. And that is to be done in order to avoid the building up of a spirit of sectionalism in Canada.

I rise to a point of order.
I have the highest respect for the hon. member, but 'he cannot put words into my mouth. I did not say that in order to avoid sectionalism the duty should be raised from 74 per cent, but I did say that the investigation which is going forward at the moment should have been completed in fairness to all parties. And that I repeat.

The hon. member may make any statement he likes, but the fact remains that the only basis upon which we can avoid sectionalism in Canada is the basis of fairness to all.. We cannot take one industry and say that it is the spoiled pet., the darling of this House of Commons or of the dominion, and that we are going to give that industry a special privilege to enable it to charge the people of Canada higher prices, and then say to another industry in western Canada, the growing of wheat, an equally important industry, that they shall grow wheat though hampered by the fact that the necessary implements cost more. There is the situation. Both sections of the dominion, all classes, must be treated on an equal basis. You cannot stand on the ground of special privilege and make an appeal on that basis in the House of Commons.
My hon. friend says that he has a great deal of sympathy for the farmer. I do not doubt that for a moment. He feels for the farmer and thinks something ought to be done for him. I respond to that and say that I have a great deal .of sympathy for the manufacturer of agricultural implements, and I contend that you cannot build up an agricultural implement industry in this country on the basis of exploited agriculture. The price of agricultural implements to-day is sixty-one per cent above the price of 1913; the price of farm products is practically the same. I want to see something done to improve the condition of the farmer, because only on the basis of an improved agriculture can we hope to have progress in Canada. On no other basis conceivable can you build up an agricultural industry in this country, and it is on that ground that I make this appeal. We must do the best we can to raise the status of agriculture, for until that is done your industries are in danger, and the one that is in greatest danger is the manufacture of agricultural implements. It cannot prosper unless agriculture is also prosperous.
Will the hon. gentleman answer this question? What was the price of wheat in 1915, 1916 and 1917 in western Canada?

The price of wheat was held at that time at an unduly low level because of government control. The price did not reach the level it would have reached had it not been for government interference. But when it comes to the other proposition, the interference is the other way.

I would not dare to correct the Minister of Finance, especially when there sit beside him those who have the facts and

figures, but I reserve the right, in all deference, to disagree with the statement he has just made. I have not the facts before me but I should like to have the privilege of looking them up.

I wish to say a word in defence of the western man and especially in support of my hon. friend from Portage la Prairie (Mr. Leader). There seems to be a great deal of controversy over this tariff question, and I want to commend the minister for this reduction, provided that it results in a reduction to the farmers. Possibly as a result of this committee's investigation there will be a reduction in the price of farm machinery, but unless that reduction is passed on to the farmers then I do not think any reduction in the tariff will amount to a row of beans. The tariff does not enter into the question to a very great extent unless in the final analysis the farmer gets the benefit. We have heard a great deal said about these prices, but unless these reductions are actually forthcoming and the farmer receives the benefit of them they will not mean a thing. We have even heard a great deal of sympathy expressed for the farmer during the last little while. Sympathy is all right, but it is pretty hard stuff to eat, especially in these hard times. Consideration has been shown for the manufacturer. I do not suggest for a moment that the manufacturer should not be allowed a reasonable profit, but I say that the profit of the agriculturist should be greater, and until this business is settled we are not going to get very far.
It has been suggested here, as a solution for unemployment, that we should revert to a back to the land movement so that the number of farmers will be increased and more grain will be raised that we shall not be able to sell, so the net return necessarily will be less. I think that is starting to work at the wrong end. Instead' of our showing so much consideration for the manufacturer lest his prices be reduced a little, I think it would be only fair to have some logical solution such as that suggested by the hon. member for Huron North. Give the farmers a little more consideration and then they will be able to buy the machinery at the price asked by the manufacturer, the price which will allow the manufacturer a profit. I do not think the tariff enters into the question very much, though I should like to see the tariff reduced provided the farmer gets a proper return for his produce and prices are lowered. So, as I say, I commend the minister for this reduction, but I hope he will go a little further and, as a result of the investigation of this

committee, see that the farmers get a square deal and a reduction in price for their farm machinery.
Mr. BENNEiTT:	I should like to say
just a word. I ask the Minister of Finance if he cannot find it possible to adopt a fairer attitude towards this matter than the one which has obtained so far. Does he not think, after having had the gasoline matter dealt with by the tariff board, it would be reasonable to have this matter also dealt with by that board? Where is a committee to get in a question of this kind? Where has a committee ever got in a matter of this kind? Only the other day it was admitted by the Minister of Trade and Commerce that a committee was no body to deal with a complex matter such as the marketing of our wheat, and that a royal commission would be better able to deal with that matter than a committee of the House of Commons. Do those who speak for the farmers here to-night think it is fair; would a farmer think it is fair; does any hon. member think it is fair, apart altogether from the question of whether the duty is too high or too low, for the government to say that parliament shall refer a matter to a committee and then, having suddenly made up its mind to take certain action, to reduce the duty by five per cent under what it was and still have the committee function, instead of referring the matter to the tariff board to deal with?
We have had several very important matters dealt with by the tariff board. Today the minister was good enough to say that the gasoline schedule was, word for word, that recommended by the tariff board, and we have two or three other items of the same kind. The basis of goodwill between two sections of the country is the thought in the minds of both that they have been treated fairly. What I put to the minister is that they have not been treated fairly, and by "fairly" I mean both having been given the opportunity to be heard before any action was taken to prejudice the position of either. In this instance the farming community presented its case with great vigour, and the government of the day has taken this action after having pointed out that the matter might be left for the Minister of Finance to deal with in his budget. But there is still time to refer the matter to the tribunal which has been set up for that purpose.
When my hon. friends were talking as they were a few moments ago, about the price of wheat, I would remind them that to-day the farmer is receiving 87J cents a

Customs Tariff
bushel for wheat that is being sold for 774 cents a bushel. That is the position to-day. There is a fixed price of 874 cents for the farmers' wheat, and that same wheat is being sold for 774 cents. *
What about 1932?

I am talking about
to-day. How would the farming population like it if, to-morrow morning, parliament declared that this 874 cents was wiped out; that there would be no longer any fixed price with respect to wheat and that the whole matter would1 be adjusted on the basis mentioned by the hon. member for Huron North, namely, the world market? Would they not say that was an unfair thing to do? Would these hon. gentlemen who have spoken to-night not say that? Would they not complain bitterly about any such action? I think they would, and properly so. All I suggest, without giving any expression of opinion as to whether this duty is high or low-I have refrained from that-is this: In all fairness why not leave this matter to the tariff board? This committee will get nowhere; it cannot possibly get anywhere with this question. No committee ever has got anywhere with a matter of this kind. Does the minister not recall the committee of this house that dealt with gasoline, when thousands and thousands of dollars were spent in the payment of auditors? To-day a committee is sitting. Since the committee began to sit we have been paying $50 a day for a lawyer and $50 a day for an auditor, I am informed. That makes $100 a day being paid out for an auditor and a lawyer, and does anyone suggest for a moment that they are ever going to be able to reach any conclusion which will be of value to this house or to this country?
This is the only suggestion I have to make, but I desire to impress it upon the minister with all possible force: We should treat these interests fairly, even as the farmers expect to be treated fairly with respect to the price that is fixed to-day for the wheat they sell. They would complain, and properly so, if their rights were taken from them in regard to that fixed price. So these implement companies have a right to present their case to the tribunal set up for that purpose. There is an excise tax of three per cent which to all intents and purposes amounts to an additional duty, making the total 104 per cent, but of course conditions are vastly different from what they were in 1924. It will be recalled that the then president of one of the largest implement companies came to this city and presented his case on behalf of the workmen,
not on behalf of the capital involved. That was his whole plea, the welfare of the men employed.
I am not here to add anything to what has been said by hon. members of this committee, nor am I going to attempt to rebut the statements they have made. I desire to urge upon the minister, however, that he give fair play; that we may do what is decent and right and fair with respect to all the industries of the country, not with respect to one but with respect to all, and that we shall not in connection with one say that we shall leave it to a board and in connection with another say we shall act in an arbitrary way. Let us create a feeling of confidence, alike in the east and in the west so that if the board finds, on a certain set of facts, that a certain condition exists and, in the terms of the tariff act, that a certain schedule would give all the protection necessary for the preservation of that industry in the country, then we know the exact situation; we have a clear and comprehensive view of it, just as we have in connection with gasoline based upon the report we heard this afternoon. But to have one section of Canada believe it is singled out for treatment entirely at variance with that accorded to another section is to create, on the one hand, a feeling of suspicion and distrust and, on the other, to give the agrarian in the west the idea that laws are made for him to impose his will upon particular people with respect to matters which are very dear to him and with respect to the prices of articles which he has to purchase. I say that is not fair and I am pleading for fairness. That is all.
In view of all that has been said it would be highly improper for me, because of the conflict of opinions and views, and what has been said with respect to the 74 per cent and three per cent duty, to express an opinion as to the adequacy or inadequacy of this particular item. But I can see no reason why the agricultural implement business of this country should not be given an opportunity to present its case before the tribunal created by law to examine such matters, nor why a committee of the house, after the duty has been reduced by five per cent, should continue to pay a lawyer and an auditor $100 a day for the two of them when in the ultimate analysis they will not be able to make a single contribution to the solution of the problem. I submit that to the minister, and trust he will realize that, in doing so, I have no object except that, having lived in western Canada as long as I have, and knowing how the feelings of the western agrarian have been played on in the past, how he has been made to think of the agricultural implement makers as men who are lying in wait to snatch from him his hard-
Customs Tariff

earned money, I desire that a feeling of confidence should be restored, by both sides believing that the tribunal will give fair, complete and patient consideration and attention to every argument that can be adduced. If the government think it desirable to appoint counsel to represent the agrarian interest I would be content that this should be done. But to go ahead with the reduction of five aer cent without notice or without a chance to be heard being given, while briefs were oeing submitted to a committee of the house, is at variance with the usual course, and to Say now that the committee is to continue, and that the board that was created for the purpose of hearing evidence is not to hear it, is in my judgment to go a long way towards creating suspicion, unrest and distress and to increase the intensity of the feeling, if there be any, between those who toil on the soil in the west and those who produce agricultural implements in the east.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: The questions addressed to myself I must of course endeavour to answer. The principle laid down by the leader of the opposition is one which has an appeal, and he put it in its most appealing form. I would, however, point out to him that the enactment of the tariff board legislation at no time was intended, even by himself, to take from the government of the day the responsibility and the opportunity of making such changes in the tariff as in their judgment were in the best interests of the people of Canada.
I do not suggest that it was.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext:
In the case of the gasoline inquiry, to which reference has been made, we were fortunate enough to have a complete report available, so that parliament might be given that report and given the facts in great detail upon which the government based its proposal to parliament. In connection with certain aspects of the textile industry the same is true. With respect to a number of other proposals now before the committee, no recommendation of the tariff board is available, but the usual machinery of government, machinery which has functioned for many years in connection with the tariff, has been used upon which to base the judgment of the government as to what should be proposed to the house and to this committee. Perhaps my right hon. friend will permit me to say that his observations with regard to fairness should work both ways. That is, the principles which he lays down surely should apply with respect to the increase of the tariff by governmental action if they are to be applied to the

decrease of it. May I remind him that in 1930, without any tariff board, without any expert advice, the tariff was raised to great heights on some three hundred items of the schedules, if my- memory is correct.
With respect to the item under discussion- and I want to stay within the rules and stick to that item-the tariff was raised from the 6 per cent level at which it had stood for several years, a level from which, as the hon. member for Huron-Perth (Mr. Golding) said this afternoon, the Massey-Harris company [DOT] did not request an increase before the tariff board prior to 1930; that tariff was raised by one act of the government of which my right hon. friend wTas the leader from six to twenty-five per cent. Then, on top of that twenty-five per cent came the additional three per cent special excise. It is true that my right hon. friend will say: We took an undertaking from the manufacturers that they would not increase prices.

Which undertaking they
lived up to.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext:
To which I believe they lived up to the letter. But that, may I point out, is not sufficient to meet the condition as between the primary producer and the1 secondary producer. When the primary producer has to bear the weight of constantly decreasing values for what he produces, what good is it to him to have an assurance that the things he buys will merely not be increased in price? What we must strive to bring about in this country-and I know my right hon. friend desires it as much as any of us-is a greater approach to parity between the return secured by our people engaged in primary production as compared with the return received by those engaged in other classes of production and in distribution. It is well known that things are out of balance not only in this country 'but in the country to the south and in many countries in the world. I agree with my right hon. friend when he says that these adjustments which must be made are far better approached from the basis of scientific analysis and examination than by appeal to the passions of the classes who are suffering from these extremes. I join with my right hon. friend in the belief that careful, consistent and steady examination should be made of these problems, not in the atmosphere of the hustings or even of parliament, but rather in the atmosphere which it has been sought to create by a tribunal such as the tariff board. I can speak for the government when I say that if the farm implement industry of Canada wishes to have the matter of farm implement duties referred to the tariff board it has only to ask for this and the reference will be made.

Customs Tariff
As to what this house is doing through the committee which is now investigating,-not the tariff on agricultural implements-I call the attention of the hon. member for Greenwood (Mr. Massey) to that-but the reason why immediately after a reduction in the tariff an increase in prices took place, is that not important? Hon. members1 representing the constituencies from one end of Canada to the other where these implements are bought and used would not be doing their duty by their constituents unless they insisted upon immediate action to find out why that increase was necessary. No adequate explanation has so far been given. It will be a good thing for the manufacturers of agricultural implements to place their facts before those men in this house who represent the farmers of this country. Surely nothing but good can come from a knowledge of the facts by the men who sit in this house representing the people of constituencies which use in such large measure the products of agricultural implement factories. I join with my right hon. friend in the belief that there has been too great a gap of misunderstanding between industry on the one hand and agriculture on the other, but I submit that before a committee of this house they can get together; they may at least agree on the facts. As far as the industry itself is concerned, it can have a reference to the tariff board at any time it applies to the present Minister of Finance for one. And the government will endeavour to see, in that connection as in all others, that the facts are brought out, in order that there may be made to this house a report in which all hon. members may have confidence because it has been produced in an atmosphere as little contentious and as non-political as possible.
I would point out, however, that the government have not gone the length of putting the duty on agricultural implements back to the point at which it was when the former Liberal government left office in 1930. Many supporters of this government believe that that should have been done. But in the light of prevailing conditions our best judgment was that the 7h per cent rate which appears throughout the whole agricultural implement schedule was a proper rate at which to put the duty during this session, of parliament. I fully expect, indeed I hope that the agricultural implement industry will apply for a tariff board reference. If they do, then by the time this house meets again we shall surely have available-at least I hope we shall-a mass of facts which are not a matter of dispute between members from this constituency and from that, but which may be agreed upon as facts, whatever may be the
respective opinions of hon. members as to the policy which should be based upon those facts.

The leader of .the opposition made an appeal to hon. members representing agricultural constituencies, and particularly those from the western provinces. As the Minister of Finance has said, I think the appeal was very well directed. However I should like to draw the attention of the leader of the opposition to considerations which compel us to discuss this matter in the House of Commons and to make the representations that have been made not only from this corner but from other sections of the house.
I have before me two tables, one of which was compiled by the Searle Grain Company of Winnipeg, giving an index of prices paid, and values received, in western Canada between 1913 and 1935. Taking the index of No. 1 hard wheat for the year 1913-14 as 100, we find that in 1935 the price had fallen to 93. Of course that is considerably better than the relative index of 52 of 1933. We have to remember, however, that in 1935 the set price to which the right hon. gentleman referred was operative. On .the other hand, taking 100 as the index figure of what the farmers bought in 1913-14 we find that it had risen in 1935 to 125, considering 147 articles farmers buy. Again, taking 100 as the index of the farmers' purchasing power in 1913-14, we find that in 1935 it had fallen to 74. The bureau of statistics index of farm implement prices shows them to be entirely out of line, because in 1935 farm implements were 54 per cent higher, on the average, than they were in 1913-14, and tools and hand implements used in agriculture were 76 per cent higher. Because of this condition pressure is quite properly brought to bear upon, the government and private members to deal with the situation. It seems to me that in the light of these considerations the government has done the right thing in reducing .the duty at the present time.
While one readily admits that implement manufacturers may be able and should have an opportunity to make out a case, nevertheless I believe immediate action has been required of this government and of this parliament. I place the figures quoted before the committee to show that it is not in a spirit of captious criticism .that we urge the reduction in the prices of implements and the duties thereon, but because we believe that the prices charged for agricultural implements are quite out of line with those received for other commodities, particularly

remembering the reduced cost of basic raw material, and of labour involved in the production of farm implements. If we are wrong, then as the Minister of Finance has said, the companies should prepare their case and present it with the assurance that they will be given fair consideration.
There are two matters I should like to clear up-
Before the item carries-
I have been on the floor half a dozen times. Am I so small that I cannot be seen.

speakerposition: Deputy Speaker and Chair of Committees of the Whole of the House of Commons
speechtext: The hon. member for Huron-Perth has the floor at the moment.
All right; go to it.

Before the item passes there are two or three points I should like particularly to stress. The hon. member for Greenwood complains that I quoted figures from 1924 to 1930 and did not take into consideration the depression from 1932 to the present time. In answer to that I should like to say that the point which prompted me to rise this afternoon was the statement made by the hon. member for Davenport as to the "disastrous" results which followed the reduction of the tariff in 1924. That was my reason for quoting figures showing a comparison of the period between 1924 and 1930 with the period between 1930 and 1934. Under the circumstances I believe I was justified in quoting the figures.
I made reference to the 18,000 employees mentioned by the hon. member for Greenwood, employees whose jobs it was said would be placed in jeopardy by a reduction of the tariff. Speaking on that point the hon. member said that it did not matter whether there was 18,000 or 9,000. I suggest . it is important that we be careful when we quote figures of that kind, because no hon. member should exaggerate. I do not question the sincerity of the hon. member for Greenwood, but I suggest he must take the figures as they are. The figures I quoted were those which were submitted to the price spreads commission and had reference to the four largest and ten smaller implement companies. Those figures showed that at that time there were only 3,880 people employed in implement factories representing about ninety-two per cent of the total production. In my opinion that is an important fact.
I believe there is and has been an effort to stampede the industrial worker by making him believe that any reduction in tariff is going to affect his position seriously, and in

view of that we ought to be careful when we quote figures. The hon. member for Parkdale complained about my having quoted figures from the bureau of statistics and asked me why I would not quote my own figures. I contend that if from my place in the house I had quoted figures and when the hon. member had asked me what figures I was quoting, I had replied, "these are my own figures," he would have been one of the first to challenge them.
They might be just as reliable.

I suggest that when we quote figures supplied by the bureau of statistics, surely to goodness hon. members opposite cannot question them. They are the only figures which we can quote.
One further point is that if it is claimed the raising or lowering of tariffs will either help or ruin the agricultural industry, then I contend that the figures we have before us for the different periods of years show that reductions in tariffs help the industry, the employee and the working man. The hon. member for Greenwood has said: "Between 1930 and 1935 this company experienced a loss of $25,700,000." Was that loss sustained during a time when there was a lowering of duties or was it sustained when duties were being increased? The fact of the matter is, as the figures show, that the companies and the industrial workers suffered more after the tariffs were increased than they ever did under a reduction of tariffs. That is all I have to say on the matter.

At last I have a chance
to say a word or two. After listening to the eloquent remarks of the Minister of Finance (Mr. Dunning), and of my honoured leader (Mr. Bennett), who is a wonderful debater, I am diffident about saying anything at all. Although I have some business ideas of my own which I try to express to the house, I find at times a gfreat deal of difficulty in saying just what I think. That will not prevent me from saying some things that I think.
I do not agree with the hon. member for Rosetown-Biggar (Mr. Coldwell) that it was proper to reduce the duty on farm implements. In fact, the training which I have had in the business world leads me to think it is a bad thing either to lower or to raise duties, because to do so always puts some people in some lines of business into difficulties, so that if the government would stop tinkering'with everything all the time, and let us go ahead, we should do better still.
We have listened in this house to economists of all kinds. I am a member of the

Customs Tariff
agriculture committee which is investigating the prices of farm implements. I am also one who tries to save the money of the country as he would try to save his own, and I protested against the system adopted in the first place by the committee. The first day we had a meeting we listened ,to some technical highly trained doctor-I assume he was an economist-who talked over our heads; I suppose nobody but a Rhodes scholar could have understood him. We followed that up the next day with something of a similar kind, from another branch of the service. I am not condemning these people, but this is what was done. In the first place we engaged counsel at $50 a day and expenses, which I do not think was too high. Then we engaged an accountant, also at $50 a day. I do not think we need either of these gentlemen. This has been going on since March 17. Then we have two or three committee reporters, receiving, I suppose, ten or fifteen dollars a day; we have literature coming from the committee to the house every day, and we have got nowhere yet. If that is .the way in which the government carries on business it should go out of business.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext:
Not the government;
this house.

The house has very little
to say. The government is doing this. We now have only four Conservatives on the agriculture committee; we have three or four economists. An economist is like a man who gets into a big barrel, looks out through the bung-hole and imagines he can stop the falls of Niagara or bring the sun and moon to a standstill. Too many of their suggestions are impracticable. In this house we ought to get down to business and stop talking economics all the time. Economy is much more important; it is one of the things I should like to see studied, and as a rule it is not considered by this government or, I assume, by some other government.
The hon. member for Portage la Prairie (Mr. Leader) said that the hon. member for Greenwood (Mr. Massey) had made certain remarks in the interests of his riding. My contention is that any remarks he made in the interests of his riding are equally in the interests of the farmers of this country. I am just as much interested in the farmers of Canada, and particularly of Ontario, as in the workers in any other industry. They have been good friends of mine, and they have no better friend than myself as regards looking after their interests; as far as I am concerned I shall always oppose any injustice to the farmer. But he must not expect
everything; somebody else must also get consideration, because others have to live as well as he.
The hon. member for Davenport (Mr. Mac-Nicol) remarked this afternoon that everyone representing an industrial riding should rise in his place and say something in protest against the lowering of duties on farm implements. When I was in this house in 1924 I took a strong stand on that particular matter. I advanced the argument that if the duty were lowered I was afraid this would result in driving the industrial workers out of cities like Toronto and Hamilton, in the vicinity of Which I live, with the result that the people who grow commodities in the old Niagara peninsula, where I did much business, would have no one to whom to sell their stuff, because if you deplete the population of Toronto and Hamilton the farmer may as well quit growing vegetables and farm truck. It is just as much to the interests of the farmers as of any other class of the community that the industrialists should be kept busy. I tried at that time to show what would happen to the farmers, and I think my arguments were sound.
The other evening my hon. friend from Regina (Mr. McNiven) was quoting statements I made on May 1, 1924. He quoted me correctly but he did not go far enough. He quoted, as every other politician does, to suit himself, to make the other fellow look ridiculous. We all know that if the farmers are not prosperous, we in the industrial centres cannot hope for long prosperity. The same thing applies to farmers if industrial workers are unemployed, because if the people in the urban centres are without money to buy the products of the farm there is not much use growing them. So the system works both ways. What we need is cooperation in this country, and we are not getting it.

The
farmer is ready.

The extra few cents the
farmers pay on farm implements because of a duty do not amount to anything at all, when spread over some years, compared with the advantages they receive by keeping the industrial worker employed and so enabling him to buy their commodities. May I say that the farmers might take better care of their farm implements, and not leave the harrow in one field, the plough in another and the binder in a third.

How do you know?
Customs Tariff

I know because I have been in the hon. member's province of Saskatchewan and seen this. The farmers even in Ontario do the same thing. But in Saskatchewan the situation is much worse. I have been there and known men to forget where the cultivator was, where the thresher was, and everything else, and they could not find them in the spring or fall of the year when they needed them. If they took good care of their farm implements, all they paid in duties would be nothing compared with the saving in depreciation, and perhaps the country would not be in the difficulty they keep it in by growling about something all the time. I have a great deal of admiration for the hon. member for Huron-Perth (Mr. Golding), but I think without a doubt he had no conception of what is fair as between industry and the farmers. A farmer can exist better on a garden, if he grew something on his farm, than an industrial unemployed worker can do in a concrete back yard.
The hon. member forgets that the industrial worker, like the farmer, fares better under lower duties.

The industrial worker does not mind what he pays for commodities so long as he has the money to buy them with; that is the way the hon. member should feel, and the way all the country should feel, and we would all be happier. What the hon. , member needs to do is to go home and get good friends with himself.
I believe in a tariff to keep the wheels of industry rolling, but I do not believe in manufacturers taking advantage of tariffs to extract too large a profit. I am opposed to that as vigorously as I am to free trade or to anything which will interfere with the industrial workers being kept in employment. My contention is that the government should control prices. When we gave protection to the plate-glass works at Hamilton against imports that came in cheaply from Belgium, they took advantage of that protection, and my right hon. leader (Mr. Bennett) cancelled the tariff. That can be done in the case of any industry which is trying to dig gold out of the people for nothing or is making an extortionate profit.
I am a great believer in my own figures. I think I can calculate as accurately as most economists. We know that figures do not lie, but liars sometimes figure. The statistical department is not always right. You can make figures mean anything, and perhaps I have done that myself. I think the Minister of Finance is just as good at figuring as I am.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext:
But not as good at the
other thing.

I would have some difficulty in holding my own sitting round a table with him. I can remember back in 1924 when the Hon. Vincent Massey who is now High Commissioner for Canada in London was interested in the Massey-Harris company. I am not speaking disparagingly of him, but I can remember how he slept on the doorstep of the Right Hon. Arthur Meighen day after day and week after week in an effort to keep tariffs from being reduced. At that time you changed your views and you gave them a six per cent preference on the raw materials that went into the manufacture of farm implements. You fixed it up in that way. You did not put on any more duty, but you did it in another way. You always had a way of getting out of difficulties. I do not blame you for that as most of us do it as well.
At one time the Massey-Harris company was quite prosperous. That company is situated within a few yards of my former riding. I used to take in the whole of ward six but my good friend, the hon. member for Davenport, came into the house on redistribution. He redistributed me out of that part of the city of Toronto and took it to himself.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext:
There ought to be a
tariff against that.

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext:
That is
not the only wrong thing he has done.

I can remember that at
that time the Massey-Harris company employed about 4,000 people. Hon. gentlemen have been quoting statistics to show that there were only 3,500 men employed in all Canada. That is absolutely wrong. I agree with the statement made by the hon. member for Greenwood who said that 18,000 people were employed. I assume he takes in all the agents and those who go through the country to give service to the farmers, but, believe me, the agents earn their money. I know some of them sometimes drive twenty to twenty-five miles in order to sell a farmer a dollar's worth of stuff. They have to do that to keep him in good humour. All farmers and all business men are alike. I said that at one time the Massey-Harris company employed from 3,500 to 4,000 people. I knew hundreds of these employees because I lived in the vicinity of this plant for forty-five years.
The John Abel people came to Toronto from Woodridge and employed a great number of people, but they were finally forced to amalgamate with an American concern and call themselves the American Abel Company. They employed from 800 to 1,000 people, but they had to go out of business.

Customs Tariff
Their place was taken over by the American Rumley people who employ from fifteen to sixteen people to distribute tractors. That is all the good they are in this country. They are renting other parts of their building to other industries which are trying to make a living but are having a hard time. Only fifteen to twenty people are employed in this factory which at one time employed from 800 to 1,000. There is something wrong with the management of this dominion when that happens.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext:
What is wrong is the
fact that they are manufacturing something which is no longer used by the country. They are manufacturing these big tractors.

That is right. I think
the hon. gentleman knows more about what is hurting the industries of Canada than anybody else. I recently took a trip through the west, but I assume the minister has been there more often than I have. I was driven through Regina by Senator Laird and we went down to the railroad siding and saw carloads of farm implements which had come in from all parts of the United States. These implements should not have been in this country at all. If our own manufacturers had been given proper protection they would have been able to manufacture these implements. Everybody in the west thinks he should buy stuff from the United States. They believe that by their doing so the country gets the benefit of the duty, whereas if they buy from a manufacturer in Canada, he gets a profit. They hate to think of anyone getting a profit. We cannot live without a profit, and that applies to retail business, wholesale business or manufacturing. There must be something wrong with the minds of men who hate to see someone make a profit, who would rather pay a duty and buy stuff from the United States.
We all can remember in 1924 when at least two to three hundred thousand people left this country to go to the United States. We did not realize that we had any unemployment at that time because these people could find jobs over there, but the situation is different to-day. They cannot find jobs in the United States and unemployment has been increasing ever since 1929. We lost a large number of highly educated men and women who went to the United States because they had no hope of getting anything to do in Canada. There was no hope for these people who had been educated at great expense to the country. They went to the United States and helped to build up the industries of that republic; we were just an 12739-195
incubator for the United States. Professional men particularly could get jobs quite easily in the United States, sometimes when even Americans could not. Canadians were appreciated and from 1921 to 1928 or 1929 we lost the best class of Canadian citizens.
